title: ‘I’ve never been counted’: DR Congo’s first census in 42 years
summary: For many Congolese, the census is about identity, recognition and finally being recorded by the state.
full_text:
‘I’ve never been counted’: DR Congo’s first census in 42 years
For many Congolese, the census is about identity, recognition and finally being recorded by the state.
Bunia, Democratic Republic of the Congo – For Heritier Ramazani, being counted is about more than a population figure. It could be the first time the Congolese state officially recognises his existence.
The 28-year-old resident of Bunia, the capital of Ituri province in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, has never appeared in a national census and has no official document confirming his Congolese citizenship.
“I’ve never been registered in a census since I was born,” Ramazani told Al Jazeera.
“Being registered and having my identity card will make me very happy.”
His experience reflects a wider challenge in the DRC, where millions of people have grown up without official documents confirming their identity.
Now, 42 years after the country’s last census, authorities are preparing to count the population again.
The previous census was conducted in 1984, when the country was still known as Zaire. Since then, the DRC has experienced decades of political upheaval, armed conflict and rapid population growth.
The World Bank estimates the country’s population at about 112 million people, with an annual growth rate of roughly 3.2 percent.
The government says the census will provide reliable data for planning public services. For many residents, however, the issue is more immediate: being officially recorded by the state.
Identity on paper
In Bunia, where years of violence involving armed groups have displaced communities across Ituri province, access to official documents remains a major concern.
Because national identity cards have not been widely available for decades, voter registration cards have long served as one of the few widely accepted forms of identification for many Congolese.
Gedeon Katembo, a 36-year-old father of three, hopes the census will help create a stronger system for issuing identity documents.
“It is essential to know how many Congolese people there are in the country and around the world,” Katembo told Al Jazeera.
“The census can also help to strengthen national unity.”
The absence of widespread identity documents is rooted in decades of political instability, weak administrative systems and conflict that has disrupted state services across much of the country.
Counting amid conflict
The census will begin with a digital mapping exercise in which teams will identify inhabited areas before household data collection starts.
The task will be immense. The DRC covers more than 2.3 million square kilometres (888 square miles), and many communities remain difficult to reach because of poor roads, limited infrastructure and insecurity.
Henri Marie Kazadi, technical coordinator of the Central Census Office at the National Institute of Statistics, said the exercise would rely on digital tools rather than paper forms.
“The census is digital. We will be using tablets and smartphones to collect the data,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The mapping exercise is designed to prepare for the main phase of the general census. We are deploying teams of cartographers in the field to identify and geolocate all inhabited places, after which the actual census will follow.”
The Ministry of Planning, through the National Institute of Statistics and the Central Census Office, began recruiting field workers in June for the mapping phase.
But in eastern DRC, where armed groups remain active, reaching every community will be one of the biggest challenges.
Muyisa Hangi Christophe, an activist with Filimbi, a pro-democracy civic movement, said displacement could prevent many people from being counted.
“We find ourselves almost in a situation where it is impossible to organise the census,” he told Al Jazeera.
“State authority is not effectively established across the whole national territory, and there are massive population displacements, as the census requires people to be interviewed in their respective communities.”
Politics of the count
The census also comes at a politically sensitive moment.
Efforts to establish a national identification system began under former President Joseph Kabila, but the process stalled during the political crisis that followed the end of his constitutional mandate.
With general elections expected in 2028, some opposition figures and civil society groups fear population figures could become politically contested, particularly over representation and governance.
Ebuteli, a Kinshasa-based research institute, has warned that the census could become increasingly sensitive as the country debates constitutional changes and its political future.
Prince Bitaki, an opposition politician, said authorities must ensure the process is not used for political purposes.
“A census is all well and good, but why carry it out when the country is heading towards a crucial moment when we should instead be preparing for the upcoming elections?” he told Al Jazeera.
The government rejects claims that the census has political motives, saying it is a routine state exercise designed to improve national planning.
More than a headcount
For development analysts, the value of the census lies in helping authorities make decisions based on accurate population data rather than estimates.
Maneno Kakule Ndavugha, a development analyst, said the figures could help determine where schools, hospitals, roads, water systems and electricity projects are most needed.
“It makes no sense for the state to build a football stadium in an area where there are only older people,” he told Al Jazeera.
Reliable census data could help officials understand where people live, their living conditions and what services are required.
For residents such as Ramazani and Katembo, however, the census is not just about numbers. It is about finally appearing in official records and obtaining documents that many Congolese have never had.
For Katembo, official identity documents represent a form of recognition that many Congolese feel they have long lacked.
“Through these cards, we will regain the nationality we lost over 40 years ago,” Katembo told Al Jazeera.

title: Russian strikes near Ukrainian capital kill three, including child
summary: Attack comes as US Senate passes new Russia sanctions and Kyiv appeals for air defence interceptors.
full_text:
Russian strikes near Ukrainian capital kill three, including child
Attack comes as US Senate passes new Russia sanctions and Kyiv pleads for more interceptors.
Russian strikes have killed three people, including a child, in the region surrounding Kyiv, according to a Ukrainian official, as explosions rocked the capital and fires broke out across parts of the city.
The strikes hit three locations in the Boryspil district, just outside Kyiv, on Saturday, according to Tymur Tkachenko, the head of the regional administration. Three more people were wounded.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Is the conflict between Russia and Ukraine deepening?
- list 2 of 3Several killed in attacks on Ukraine as Kyiv hits Russian e-commerce giant
- list 3 of 3US Senate passes sweeping Russian energy sanctions bill amid Ukraine war
The attack was the latest in a Russian bombardment that Ukraine’s depleted air defences have been increasingly unable to stop, exposing a widening gap between Russia’s ability to attack Ukrainian cities and Kyiv’s ability to thwart those attacks.
Fires broke out in two districts of the capital after an air raid alert sounded early on Saturday. Residents in central Kyiv described powerful explosions shaking buildings nearby.
Russian ballistic missiles travel at several times the speed of sound and dive towards their targets so steeply that Ukrainian defenders often have only seconds to respond.
Patriot air defence systems, supplied by the United States, remain the only weapons in Ukraine’s arsenal able to reliably intercept them. Officials in Kyiv have said they lack anywhere near enough batteries or interceptors to shield their cities properly.
Earlier this week, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine received only a third as many air-defence missiles in the first half of this year as it had during the same period in 2025. He attributed the shortfall to the US-Israel war on Iran, which has drawn down global stockpiles of air defence interceptors.
Ukrainian government advisers estimate that Russia can now launch about 100 ballistic missiles a month, and officials have warned that Moscow is preparing to intensify its campaign further once winter sets in.
The latest Russian attacks come as Ukraine has repeatedly targeted sites deep within Russia’s territory, including two oil refineries in the last 24 hours. Ukraine also launched long-range drones at a warehouse of the online retailer Wildberries in the city of Ekaterinburg.
Attacks on Wildberries locations have been part of what Ukrainian officials have described as a campaign against logistics sites they say support Russia’s military.
Separately on Friday, the governor of Russian-occupied Crimea said that two people had been killed when a Ukrainian drone hit an apartment building.
New sanctions bill
Also on Friday, the US Senate passed a sweeping new sanctions bill targeting Russian energy exports, including 100 percent tariffs on countries still buying Russian oil and gas.
The bill, approved 86-11, was named after the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a longtime advocate of tougher measures against Russia.
The legislation would need to be passed by the House of Representatives and signed by President Donald Trump before it becomes law.
Zelenskyy welcomed the vote, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said it would help “drain Russia’s means to continue a war it cannot win”.

title: Saudi intelligence chief meets Iraqi PM, renews Riyadh visit invitation
summary: Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had cancelled an earlier Saudi trip after deadly July 29 US-Saudi strikes on Iraq.
full_text:
Saudi intelligence chief meets Iraqi PM, renews Riyadh visit invitation
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had cancelled an earlier Saudi trip after deadly July 29 US-Saudi strikes on Iraq.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Saudi Arabian Intelligence chief Khalid bin Ali Al Humaidan have met in Baghdad in an attempt to resolve the governments’ ties strained by deadly cross-border strikes weeks earlier.
Al-Humaidan extended a renewed invitation for al-Zaidi to visit Riyadh in the meeting on Friday, the prime minister’s office said, after the latter’s earlier trip was called off in protest following a joint Saudi-US operation on July 29. The attacks killed 20 fighters of Iraqi armed groups, including five Iranians.

- list 2 of 3Trump shifts blame to Republicans for waning support from public
- list 3 of 3US courts clear way for deportations of South Sudan, Myanmar nationals
According to al-Zaidi’s office, the two focused on how Baghdad and Riyadh can better coordinate security issues as regional tensions simmer.
Al-Zaidi restated a pledge that Iraqi soil would not become a launchpad for attacks on any other country, and that Baghdad remains determined to guard its sovereignty.
The two countries have had a tense few weeks of diplomacy.
Saudi Arabia justified last month’s strikes on Iraq as retaliation for drone attacks on its oil infrastructure, which it blamed on the same pro-Iranian Iraqi armed groups.
Iraq’s National Security Council rejected the kingdom’s claim outright, calling the operation a breach of national sovereignty. In the days that followed, Iraqi authorities quietly tightened security across the country and along its borders to head off any retaliation.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq – the Iran-aligned network of armed groups that has clashed rhetorically with Riyadh in recent weeks – had promised to retaliate for the US-Saudi strikes.
But it announced on Friday that it was postponing a retaliatory strike, crediting the climbdown to lobbying from Hadi al-Amiri, one of the most powerful pro-Iran voices in Iraq, along with pressure from other unnamed political figures.
The group did not say what it had been preparing to hit.
Al-Zaidi, who took office earlier this year with Washington’s backing, has pledged to bring armed groups under state control and set a September 30 deadline for them to disarm.
His call has since faced opposition from powerful factions.
Iraq has long struggled to balance its ties with both the United States and Iran. The rivalry between Washington and Tehran has repeatedly turned the country into a proxy battleground.

title: Chinese scientists find some Yangtze flood controls may do more harm than good
summary:
For centuries, the Yangtze River has been China’s vital lifeblood, yet its floods have claimed countless lives. To tame its waters, flood-control systems have evolved from ancient dykes to the engineering marvel of the Three Gorges Dam.
But a new study has uncovered a paradox: some human interventions may have inadvertently worsened the very flood risks they were built to mitigate.
“We show that flood frequency peaked during the Little Ice Age [1500−1850] … and that human interventions,...
full_text:
Chinese scientists find some Yangtze flood controls may do more harm than good
By compressing rivers and stripping away natural defences, human engineering may be worsening flood impacts, prompting a global rethink
But a new study has uncovered a paradox: some human interventions may have inadvertently worsened the very flood risks they were built to mitigate.
“We show that flood frequency peaked during the Little Ice Age [1500−1850] … and that human interventions, particularly embankments and lake reclamation, amplified climate-driven flood magnitudes,” a group of scientists in China and Europe wrote in a paper published on Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America.
They found that while climate remains the primary driver of flood occurrence, human interventions on the Yangtze River actually intensified climate-induced flood risks, rather than mitigating them.
Their analysis showed that constructing embankments and lake enclosures for agricultural use amplified the magnitude of 100-year floods, which have a 1 per cent chance of happening in any year, by 18 and 8 per cent respectively.

summary:
Trump ally Abelardo De La ‌Espriella vows to start ‘profound transformation’ of country’s destiny as he is sworn in

full_text:
The Trump administration plans to provide $1bn in security assistance to the government of Colombia’s new rightwing president, the US state department announced, soon after Abelardo De La Espriella was sworn in and used his inaugural speech to pledge a vigorous fight against drug trafficking, as well as austerity measures to restore confidence in the economy.
De La Espriella, 48, won June’s runoff election with promises to crack down on armed groups, shrink the state by as much as 40% and revive the oil and gas sector.
“I have come to close a long chapter of national resignation and, together with the people, embark on the most profound transformation of our destiny,” De La Espriella said at the Pichincha Battalion military base in Cali after being sworn in on Friday.
“I send a firm message to the Colombian people: the time has come to restore order, authority and freedom,” said De La Espriella, who received the endorsement of Donald Trump before his runoff election.
“Members of criminal gangs and narco-terrorist groups have two choices: submit to the rule of law or face the determined response of the Colombian state and its security forces,” the new president told assembled troops at the base during a 75-minute speech, adding the option of peace talks with armed groups had been “completely exhausted”.
The US state department said in a statement on Friday: “As a cornerstone of this renewed partnership, the United States, working with Congress, intends to announce $1 billion in assistance as part of a security package to support President de la Espriella’s Administration in achieving our shared goals.”
De La Espriella’s election is part of a rightward shift rippling across Latin America. In Peru, Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia and Panama, weak economies and rising crime have reshaped voter priorities, allowing once-fringe hard-right candidates to gain traction by promising crackdowns amid a global rise of rightwing nationalism.
De La Espriella could push through some of his policies via decree, but analysts say many of his proposals will require backing from a divided congress and could be watered down in negotiations.
The new president vowed to “definitively eradicate the scourge of illicit crops”, saying he would use aerial herbicides that did not harm human health or the environment to destroy coca, the plant used to make cocaine. In one of his first acts as president, Colombia would join the Shield of the Americas program founded by Trump, he said.
Before his inauguration, he held bilateral meetings with the king of Spain and the presidents of Argentina, Ecuador, Chile, Paraguay and Panama. Also attending was Gianni Infantino, the embattled head of Fifa, football’s world governing body, while the US sent a delegation headed by the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche.
De La Espriella has blamed former president Gustavo Petro, who has not recognised the new president’s victory, for an expansion of armed groups, and narrowly defeated leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda – a Petro ally – in the runoff.
Cepeda led a morning march on Friday in Barranquilla, where he told demonstrators that the country’s opposition would work to defend democracy and called for peaceful civil disobedience.
With Reuters

title: Germans hogging the sunloungers? Poll finds Italians and French are worse
summary:
British and Germans themselves share stereotype but other nationalities are likelier to put out towels – or umbrellas

Germans are sunlounger hoggers, or so the longstanding stereotype goes. But not only is that cultural trope mostly confined to British – and, even more so, German – perceptions, surprising new data reveals that in fact Italian and French holidaymakers are the ones most likely to use their towel to stake their claim to a sunlounger.

A poll by YouGov of Europeans holidaymakers found that while many Germans (51%) and Britons (46%) associate Germans with the ritual of waking up at the crack of dawn to mark their spot, the perception barely exists elsewhere in Europe, with just 5-17% of those surveyed in other countries sharing the stereotype.

full_text:
Germans are sunlounger hoggers, or so the longstanding stereotype goes. But not only is that cultural trope mostly confined to British – and, even more so, German – perceptions, surprising new data reveals that in fact Italian and French holidaymakers are the ones most likely to use their towel to stake their claim to a sunlounger.
A poll by YouGov of Europeans holidaymakers found that while many Germans (51%) and Britons (46%) associate Germans with the ritual of waking up at the crack of dawn to mark their spot, the perception barely exists elsewhere in Europe, with just 5-17% of those surveyed in other countries sharing the stereotype.
Furthermore, just 38% of German holidaymakers – as in those who stay in places that have pools and sunloungers – said they have ever reserved a lounger with a towel compared with 45% of their Italian and French counterparts. Britons were the least likely to admit to hogging a lounger (33%).
Across all countries polled, YouGov found that most people (60-82%) considered the practice unacceptable. Still, it appears to be rampant, with 51-63% saying they had found themselves deprived of a sunlounger because they were all taken, and 14-28% admitting to resolving matters by removing somebody else’s towel.
When the Guardian asked a number of Italians in Rome, nobody admitted to the practice, although they could believe the data.
“I would never do it but I have seen it happen,” said Claudia Morani, a teacher, adding that during a recent stay in a hotel with a swimming pool she had witnessed plenty of fellow Italians “leaving their towels on the loungers at the end of the day so they could use the same ones the next morning”.
Morani added: “This kind of thing happens a lot on beaches here, too – the free ones.”
Indeed, possibly even worse than sunlounger hoggers, some Italian beachgoers are cultivating a reputation as furbetti dell’ombrellone, or umbrella cheats, a name coined by the press to refer to people who leave their umbrellas pitched overnight in their quest to reserve coveted spots by the sea.
The practice is a growing trend on free-access beaches, unlike the private concessions that dominate much of Italy’s coastline during summer and from which Italians are increasingly turning away because of high prices.
Such is the extent of the problem, coastal authorities across Italy specifically target the furbetti dell’ombrellone as part of their national beach and lake safety campaign.
In late July, authorities in a suburb of Naples seized 40 items, including umbrellas, loungers and deckchairs, during a dawn sweep of a popular free beach. Similar blitzes have recently occurred on beaches in Puglia and Sardinia. Fines of up to €500 are in place for those caught, while reclaiming the confiscated personal belongings involves a bureaucratic ordeal.
“This has become a bit of a habit,” said Danilo Ruggiero, an activist with Mare Libero, a national network fighting to reclaim beaches from private concessions. “I think it’s more related to people not wanting to carry umbrellas, chairs and other equipment back and forth from home, especially in the heat. But there is a tendency to try to get the best position by the sea, and this shouldn’t be done.”
As for France, when the Guardian spoke about YouGov’s findings to two people living in the south, they were not surprised to hear that the French were partial to sunlounger hogging. “I see it all the time at my local beach club,” said Chantal Henry, who lives in Menton, close to the Italian border. “I get really fed up with it.” Her friend Virginie Pascual alleged: “It is always the Italians.”
However, a Briton living in France, who wanted to remain anonymous as they had German colleagues, was adamant Germans were by far the biggest culprits. “I saw it in Mallorca – it was 5.30am and a German dude was hogging five loungers with towels,” they said.

title: Domestic stablecoins could boost demand for dollar-backed tokens: IMF
summary: IMF first deputy managing director Dan Katz says users may favor digital dollars for their liquidity, network effects and cross-border acceptance.
full_text:
Domestic stablecoins could boost demand for dollar-backed tokens: IMF
IMF first deputy managing director Dan Katz says users may favor digital dollars for their liquidity, network effects and cross-border acceptance.
Domestic-currency stablecoins intended to curb reliance on dollar-backed tokens could instead make it easier for users to move funds into digital dollars, according to a senior International Monetary Fund (IMF) official.
On Friday, IMF First Deputy Managing Director Dan Katz said that once local and dollar stablecoins operate on the same blockchain infrastructure, users can convert between them through decentralized exchanges, liquidity pools or peer-to-peer swaps.
In a speech at the University of Cape Town, Katz said the shift could move foreign exchange activity away from banks and currency dealers, reducing the friction that gives authorities tools to monitor and manage capital flows.
“In this way, local-currency stablecoins might even accelerate the adoption of FX stablecoins,” he said.
Katz pointed to South Africa, where dollar-backed stablecoins have gained limited traction but rand-linked tokens have attracted even less demand.
While it was too early to draw firm conclusions, he said many users may favor dollar tokens because of their liquidity, network effects and acceptance across platforms and borders.
Katz said the risks vary by country. Stablecoins may largely replace existing dollar holdings in highly dollarized economies but could increase foreign-currency demand in countries where access to dollars is restricted and economic frameworks are weak.
He urged authorities to bring onramps, offramps and onchain exchange points within regulatory frameworks.
Related: Dollar stablecoins could improve FX access but amplify currency runs: IMF

full_text:
在 8 月 6 日東京高輪 Gateway City 的一家 Lawson 門市，收銀機掃了一次手機上的條碼，322 日圓的 JPYC 付款在約 5 秒內完成，收據上的付款方式印著「stablecoin」。這台 POS 機沒有為了穩定幣加裝任何硬體，結算跑在 Polygon 上，這是首次日本超商收取穩定幣的實測。
（前情提要：日本 Lawson 便利商店試點 JPYC 穩定幣支付，首次串接 POS 系統）
（背景補充：搞懂日圓穩定幣「雙軌制」未來：JPYC 的 DeFi 派與聯合穩定幣的機構派）
重點摘要
- 8/6 東京 Lawson 門市完成 322 日圓 JPYC 付款，掃碼到結束約 5 秒。
- 用既有 POS 掃條碼、不加裝硬體，結算在 Polygon 上，店家免自管錢包。
- 8/17 進第二階段，改在大崎門市支援 MetaMask，幣種擴到 USDC、USDT。
322 日圓，大概是一個御飯糰加一瓶茶的價錢。這是日本便利商店史上第一筆穩定幣付款的金額。
8/6 在東京高輪 Gateway City 的 Lawson 門市，一名顧客開啟手機錢包出示條碼，店員拿起收銀機的掃描器掃過去，約 5 秒後畫面顯示完成。列印出來的收據上，付款方式那一欄寫的是「stablecoin」。
這場實證由 HashPort 主導，KDDI 與 Lawson 一起參與，三方在 7/10 就簽好基本協議。用的穩定幣是 JPYC，日本第一個拿到金融廳資金移動業者登記的日圓穩定幣。
收銀機不必改裝
整件事最值得注意的地方，是那台收銀機什麼都沒改。
顧客端用的是 HashPort Wallet，一個非託管錢包，也就是私鑰握在使用者自己手上、服務商碰不到資產的那種。店家端則是把 HashPort Wallet for Biz 嵌進既有的 POS 系統，門市不必自己開錢包、也不必管理錢包。
中間傳導層是 PAYTREE，Canal Payment Service 旗下的多碼支付閘道。條碼掃進去之後，PAYTREE 把付款資料轉給錢包服務商驗證餘額並授權，最後在 Polygon 上完成結算。
HashPort 說這同時也是日本第一筆免 gas 費（gasless）的穩定幣付款，使用者不用另外準備鏈上手續費用的代幣。這兩項「日本首次」的宣稱目前都還沒有第三方查核。
對零售業來說，這個架構的意義解決了落地障礙，店家不用換整套裝置、重新訓練店員。
一般顧客還不能使用
但也別把場面想得太大，這次實測只開放三家公司的員工參與，走進門市的一般客人還不能用 JPYC 結帳。
JPYC 本身的規模同樣還在起步。它 2025 年 10 月 27 日才正式開始發行，7/10 時鏈上流通額剛突破 20 億日圓，目前部署在 Kaia、Polygon、Ethereum、Avalanche 四條鏈上。JPYC 代表取締役岡部典孝喊出的目標，是三年內把發行餘額做到 10 兆日圓。
從 322 日圓到 10 兆日圓，中間隔著的已經不是技術問題，是有多少人願意在超商結帳時掏出錢包裡的 JPYC。
17日換 MetaMask 上場
第二階段實測已經排好了，8 月 17 日將在 Lawson Gate City 大崎 Atrium 店，這次要支援 MetaMask 錢包，可用幣種從 JPYC 擴到 USDC 與 USDT。
HashPort 後續還規劃加入多錢包支援與隱私支付功能，應用場景則往餐飲、零售與服務業擴張。關東地區已有兩家牙科診所在試點匯入。
高輪 Gateway City 這家門市本身就是 KDDI 與 Lawson 合作的未來型店鋪「Real×Tech LAWSON」，本來就是拿來試新東西的地方。把日本第一筆便利商店穩定幣付款放在這裡跑，位置選得剛剛好。
常見問題
JPYC 是什麼？
JPYC 是日本第一個取得金融廳資金移動業者登記的日圓穩定幣，2025 年 10 月 27 日開始發行，與日圓維持 1:1 價值，目前部署在 Kaia、Polygon、Ethereum、Avalanche 四條鏈上。
一般人現在可以在 Lawson 用穩定幣付款嗎？
還不行。8/6 的實證只開放 HashPort、KDDI、Lawson 三家公司員工參與，一般顧客無法使用。8/17 的第二階段將在大崎門市進行，並擴大支援 MetaMask 與 USDC、USDT。

title: XRPL 加密轉帳上線！5.3 億美元代幣化資產準備隱形
summary:
XRP Ledger 版本 3.3.0 引入「加密轉帳」修正案，讓機構可以在不公開餘額與轉帳金額的前提下進行代 […]

〈XRPL 加密轉帳上線！5.3 億美元代幣化資產準備隱形〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
XRP Ledger 版本 3.3.0 引入「加密轉帳」修正案，讓機構可以在不公開餘額與轉帳金額的前提下進行代幣化資產交易。XRPL 上目前已有 13.8 億美元 RWA，RLUSD 與 Ondo 佔最大比例。
（前情提要：華爾街重磅實驗：摩根大通、萬事達卡聯手 Ripple，在 XRPL 完成首筆跨境代幣化國債結算）
（背景補充：Ripple 推出企業後臺管理 XRP 和法幣，瞄準年 13 兆美元企業數位資產金庫系統）
瑞波旗下 XRP Ledger 本週推出版本 3.3.0，內含六項待投票修正案，其中最引人注目的是「加密轉帳」（Confidential Transfers）功能，讓機構使用者在進行代幣化資產交易時，可以選擇加密餘額與轉帳金額，而不暴露交易規模。
這項功能不是全面啟用，而是選擇性加入。帳戶地址與代幣型別仍然可見，但個別餘額與每筆付款金額可以被加密。底層使用零知識證明技術：帳本可以驗證交易有效且收支平衡，但無法讀取背後的數字。
目前 XRPL 上已經有足夠的代幣化資產讓這個功能有實際意義。鏈上資料聚合器 RWA.xyz 追蹤顯示，XRPL 上的分散式真實世界資產（RWA）總量約為 13.8 億美元，其中：
- Ripple 穩定幣 RLUSD：8.457 億美元
- Ondo Finance：2.126 億美元
- VERT Capital：1.161 億美元
- Archax：5,540 萬美元
- Societe Generale（法國社會通用銀行）：1,160 萬美元
扣除 RLUSD 後，剩餘超過 5.3 億美元的代幣化資產主要集中在少數發行者手上。這些資產，基金、債券、機構投資工具，正是 Confidential Transfers 的標的。
為什麼機構需要「隱形」餘額？
公開帳本透明性是加密貨幣的核心賣點，但對傳統金融機構而言，公開每一筆餘額與轉帳金額反而成了障礙。
一隻共同基金不想讓市場看到它的現金位置；一家銀行不想讓競爭對手知道它的流動性配置；企業財務部門也不想讓外界追蹤它每日的資金排程。Confidential Transfers 讓 XRPL 在保留帳本可驗證性的同時，為機構使用者提供與傳統銀行系統類似的餘額隱私。
Ripple 在 2026 年花了大量時間推 XRPL 進軍代幣化金融。英國保險投資巨頭 Aviva Investors 上月推出了其美元流動性基金的代幣化股份類別，該專案是在今年二月與 Ripple 宣布合作的。
第一版功能範圍有限
Confidential Transfers 的首版設計相當保守。持有人必須主動選擇加密格式，目前僅支援 Multi-Purpose Token（MPT）帳戶間的直接支付。
它還不包括 XRPL 內建交易所的掛單交易、託管（escrow）或支票（checks）功能。也就是說，機構可以「隱形地」互轉代幣，但在 DEX 上下單的數量仍然是公開的。
另外五項修正案，同樣瞄準企業使用者
版本 3.3.0 包含的另外五項修正案也全數針對機構場景：
- Batch（批次交易）：一次打包最多八筆交易，包含「全有或全無」模式，所有步驟成功才過帳，任一失敗整筆取消
- Sponsor（費用贊助）：讓一個帳戶代另一個帳戶支付交易費用與押金要求，新使用者不需先持有 XRP 就能交易
- Permission Delegation（許可權委派）：帳戶授權另一方只能提交指定的交易型別，基金管理者取得有限許可權而不交出全部控制權
- Dynamic MPT（動態 MPT）：發行者可以在發行之後修改代幣的某些屬性
版本 3.3.0 也包含一系列修補，XRPL Operations 表示記憶體使用量削減了至少 10% 到 15%，節點同步速度也有改善。
真正考驗是後續
目前沒有任何一項修正案生效。XRPL 的修正案機制要求至少 80% 的可信驗證節點支援，且必須連續維持至少兩週才會啟用。
Confidential Transfers 接下來要過的就是這個投票門檻。投票透過後的第二道考驗更具現實意義，Aviva、Ondo 或其他已經在 XRPL 上發行資產的機構，是否真的會選擇隱藏餘額與轉帳規模，而非繼續讓所有資料公開。
市場觀察：XRPL 的代幣化路線圖正在收斂
XRPL 這波更新透露了一個明確訊號：Ripple 不再只是推 XRP 作為支付橋樑，而是在把整個帳本打造成機構級的代幣化金融基礎設施。
從 2026 年 5 月摩根大通與萬事達卡在 XRPL 上完成首筆跨境代幣化國債結算，到 RLUSD 穩定幣上線，再到現在引入餘額加密功能，路徑是一致的，把傳統金融機構最在意的三個問題一次解決：
- 能不能在公鏈上做合規的代幣化資產？（MPT + Dynamic MPT）
- 餘額與交易規模會不會被外人看到？（Confidential Transfers）
- 能不能降低新使用者的上鏈門檻？（Sponsor + Batch）
如果 Confidential Transfers 順利透過且機構採用率上升，XRPL 將成為少數在「透明性」與「隱私」之間做出制度性妥協的公鏈。這個取捨會吸引傳統金融，也會引起加密純潔主義者的批評，這本身就是一個值得觀察的張力。

title: Life as a Wag in the transfer window
summary: What is life like for footballers' families during the transfer window where a last-minute deal means you need to uproot your life and move hundreds of miles?
full_text:
Life as a Wag in the transfer window
- Published
"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."
Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.
And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.
"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.
"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."
This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).
While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.
Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.
"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."
But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.
The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.
Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.
"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.
Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.
"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.
They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.
"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.
She also had to quit her job.
"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.
Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.
"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.
"In that moment I did feel really out of control."
Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.
But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.
"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.
"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.
"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."
Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.
Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.
Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.
"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.
"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."
1 of 5
For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.
She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.
"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.
"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.
"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."
This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.
"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.
"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.
"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us."
Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.
"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.
"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."
While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.
"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.
"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.
"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."
Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.
"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.
"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.
"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.
"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.
"In football things can be really positive or really negative."
The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.
"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.
Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.
"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.
"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.
"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.
"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

title: NBA star Brandon Clarke died from heroin, cocaine effects, examiner rules
summary: Memphis Grizzlies ⁠forward Brandon Clarke's ⁠May 11 death ruled accidental, with effects of heroin and cocaine cited.
full_text:
NBA star Brandon Clarke died from heroin, cocaine effects, examiner rules
Memphis Grizzlies forward Brandon Clarke’s May 11 death ruled accidental, with effects of heroin and cocaine cited.
The Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner reported on Friday that Memphis Grizzlies forward Brandon Clarke died due to the effects of heroin and cocaine.
The medical examiner ruled Clarke’s May 11 death an accident. The combined effects of multiple prescription medications were also identified as a significant contributing condition, though the specific medications were not disclosed. The full medical examiner’s report has not yet been released.

Clarke, 29, was discovered unresponsive in a bedroom at a residence in California’s San Fernando Valley and was pronounced dead at the scene by paramedics. The medical examiner conducted an examination the following day before formally certifying the cause and manner of death on Friday.
Clarke spent his seven-year NBA career with Memphis after finishing his college career at Gonzaga. He averaged 10.2 points and 5.5 rebounds over 309 games (50 starts) and finished fourth in Rookie of the Year voting in 2019-20.
Injuries limited Clarke during his final seasons. He missed more than a year after tearing an Achilles tendon in 2023 and appeared in only two games during the 2025-26 campaign because of knee and calf ailments.
About six weeks before his death, Clarke was arrested in Arkansas on charges that included possession and trafficking of a controlled substance following a traffic stop.
Following Clarke’s death, the Grizzlies remembered him as an “outstanding teammate and an even better person” whose influence extended beyond the organisation and into the Memphis community.

title: Hundreds camp on sweltering Rome street amid tussle over squatted building
summary: After a fire broke out, the building was cleared in what activists say was a politically motivated move.
full_text:
Hundreds camp on sweltering Rome street amid tussle over squatted building
After a fire broke out, the building was cleared in what activists say was a politically motivated move.
Rome, Italy – Ana Bizdoaca has stopped expecting to be able to sleep on a mattress on the pavement a few streets from Rome’s Termini station. A heatwave has pushed temperatures past 40 degrees Celsius (104F).
“Our hearts have been torn to pieces,” Bizdoaca said on the ninth night of missing sleep.

list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4A safe space for Gaza women: A sanctuary to speak, heal and share amid war
- list 2 of 4Dangerous summers: How heatwaves and wildfires change life across Europe
- list 3 of 4Spain imposes border checks on Italy as countermeasure in Ceuta spat
- list 4 of 4Pope Leo urges migrant protection, integration on visit to Lampedusa
Around her, some 300 people, including vulnerable people and about 100 children, from across the world, are doing the same.
Behind them stands the seven-storey former office block known as Spin Time, a squatted building where they all lived until days ago. Bizdoaca has lived there since 2013.
First occupied in 2013, it became home to many, including 140 families from more than 20 countries. It started with a simple idea at its centre: housing as a fundamental right.
The residents have been outside since July 29, when a small fire broke out in the evening in a lower floor room where nobody lived. Residents put it out within minutes, before the fire brigade arrived, and the damage was minimal.
Police evacuated the building and magistrates placed it under judicial seizure. It was declared unfit, and residents are now let back in one at a time, escorted by police, only to collect documents and essentials.
The pavement has become home to the sit-in.
Food arrives at lunchtime from volunteers in the surrounding district, along with water, mattresses, and clothes. Thousands have passed through over the past nine days, including dozens of politicians, singers and actors. In the evenings, an open-air cinema gives the camp’s children something to watch other than the street.
On the first night, many did not have shoes. At 4am, they were told they would not be let back in.
“Some of us were on our feet for 40 hours,” said Maria Cabrera, who has lived in the building for almost 11 years and helps organise the camp.
“Seeing the children on the ground, on flattened cardboard from the bins, it was awful. It really was.”
On August 6, a two-year-old girl fainted in a Red Cross nurse’s arms.
“I cried for two hours,” said a Kurdish resident, who watched the scene unfold.
She told Al Jazeera that her brother, also a resident of the building, is blind and uses a wheelchair. Neighbours used to check on him while she was at work. Now, he sits under the scorching sun.
The community has drawn support from well beyond the neighbourhood.
On Friday, the physicist Giorgio Parisi, who won the Nobel Prize in 2021, sent the residents a letter.
“Inequality and marginalisation are the woodworm eating away at our democracy”, he wrote, “and we should all be on the side of those who fight them concretely, not just in words”.
‘It became a family’
Cabrera arrived a year after losing her job, having been unable to pay rent.
“At the beginning, it wasn’t simple, because there are 27 different nationalities here,” she said. “But it became family. Whoever is on my floor, I can go and ask them for anything.”
One of Rome’s most active cultural spaces, Spin Time has a free co-working area, a newspaper put together by people aged below 30, and hosts concerts and plays.
Cabrera saw her first classical music show here.
“Things I could never have afforded outside,” she said.
In 2019, the building made headlines worldwide when the pope’s almoner, Cardinal Konrad Krajewski, descended into a manhole to restore electricity, which had been cut due to mounting debts.
An irrevocable no
On August 3, Rome’s prefect convened the mayor, police chief, housing councillor and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, vicar general of the Diocese of Rome.
The city offered to buy the building from InvestiRE SGR, the fund that manages it, with an interim arrangement that would let residents return while the sale went through.
Another meeting was held on Thursday. Mayor Roberto Gualtieri announced live on television that the offer had been rejected.
“I’m not happy, and I’m somewhat irritated,” he said, adding that the Church had done everything it could to persuade them.
The city is now working on an alternative.
In a statement issued late on Thursday, InvestiRE SGR said that the inspection confirmed that after 13 years of occupation, the building does not meet safety standards and that this legally precludes handing possession to the city, thereby ruling out any interim arrangement.
The company added that it remains willing to continue talks towards selling the building.
Gualtieri said the city would be able to place residents in dignified accommodation from Monday, and that the first housing assignments could begin within 60 days for households that qualify.
But the activists, who want to stay, say they will hold the sit-in as long as possible to pressure the local government.
The fund has long planned a luxury hotel on the site, and Spin Time has for years been listed by the government as a site to be cleared.
The governing right-wing Brothers of Italy party pressured the mayor not to proceed with the purchase, saying using public money as thousands wait on housing lists would reward illegality.
“We never thought they would use this tragedy” to evacuate the building, Aurora Jacob, another resident, said of populist forces. “Someone took advantage of an emergency, of the vulnerability of families and children, to push them out of their homes. The difference between us and you is that we are second-class citizen.”
‘I don’t think being poor is a crime’
The Vatican is now watching from a distance.
Pope Leo XIV recently received members of the community. Cardinal Reina has said the pope asks to be updated hour by hour.
If a permanent eviction goes ahead, Spin Time would be the largest occupation to face such measures in Italy.
Asked what she wants now, Cabrera does not hesitate.
“A miracle,” she said. “I don’t think being poor is a crime.”
The authorities should stop playing with people who need help, she said, and the owners should finally sell.
“Everyone is just speculating, on the price of a building and on us, on people going through difficult times.”
She gestured back at the dark windows above the mattresses.
“It’s not a luxury home. We put up four walls,” she said. “But for us, that is home. And we want to go back.”

title: Bangladesh say Shakib will not play cricket again after Hasina event
summary: Shakib Al Hasan says he will return home to face trial if safety assured, but Bangladesh rule out cricket comeback.
full_text:
Bangladesh say Shakib will not play cricket again after Hasina event
Shakib Al Hasan says he will return home to face trial if safety assured, but Bangladesh rule out cricket comeback.
Bangladesh have said former star cricketer Shakib Al Hasan had no prospect of returning to play after he joined a media event with ousted former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, a convicted fugitive.
Shakib joined the event by telephone in New Delhi on Wednesday, where Hasina addressed journalists, two years after she was forced from power following a deadly crackdown on student-led protests.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Argentina and Mexico back Infantino, deepening FIFA divide: What to know
- list 2 of 4Infantino, FIFA try to move beyond botched World Cup sell-off: What we know
- list 3 of 4UEFA’s threatened legal action against Infantino and FIFA: What we know
- list 4 of 4UEFA confirms legal letter served to FIFA after Infantino’s World Cup plan
Bangladesh Minister for Youth and Sports Aminul Haque said the government had previously taken a more open approach towards Shakib, who was a politician for Hasina’s former ruling Awami League party.
Shakib, who is currently in Sri Lanka, was among dozens facing murder investigations for a deadly police crackdown on protesters that toppled Hasina’s government.
“We had been looking at the matter with considerable flexibility and tolerance. After this, I do not think there is any room to think that way anymore,” Haque said in a statement.
“Someone who has taken the stage with the autocrat no longer has any opportunity to return.”
Shakib, 39, is Bangladesh’s most successful cricketer and one of the country’s best-known sporting figures. He has played more than 400 international matches and represented Bangladesh at five World Cups.
Rights groups have long accused Hasina’s former administration of abuses including the murder of rivals, suppression of opposition parties, rigged courts and one-sided elections.
A court in Dhaka found Hasina guilty in absentia in November 2025 of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to be hanged. She remains in hiding in India.
All-rounder Shakib announced his retirement plans in September 2024 after his team’s second Test in India but later said he would play a full series before calling it quits.
The Bangladesh Cricket Board said in January he could play again, but his involvement in the event in India on Wednesday caused anger, with Shakib saying his house had been petrol-bombed as a result.
On Thursday, Shakib said he was prepared to return to Bangladesh from his exile in Sri Lanka to face trial on charges including murder. He also said he hoped to play for his country again at the 2027 Cricket World Cup, having led the team at the last edition in 2023.

title: FIFA’s Infantino backed in Colombia where he attends president inauguration
summary: FIFA president Gianni Infantino gets South American football's backing while at Abelardo de la Espriella's inauguration.
full_text:
FIFA’s Infantino backed in Colombia where he attends president inauguration
FIFA President Gianni Infantino gets South American football’s backing while at Abelardo de la Espriella’s inauguration.
FIFA president Gianni Infantino has received support from several leading South American football figures as he visited Colombia amid the crisis engulfing world football’s governing body.
Infantino arrived early on Friday in the Colombian city of Cali to attend the inauguration ceremony of hard-right President Abelardo de la Espriella.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Diego Maradona bloated, bedridden and resigned before death, says masseur
- list 2 of 4Cricketer Shakib, an Hasina ally, will face trial in Bangladesh if secure
- list 3 of 4Saudi Pro League’s England international Toney charged with assault
- list 4 of 4Africa backs Infantino as CAF unanimously votes in FIFA president’s favour
Photos released by the Colombian Football Federation show a smiling Infantino standing alongside South American Football Confederation (CONMEBOL) president Alejandro Dominguez and the president of the Colombian federation, Ramon Jesurun.
The visit to Colombia comes as the head of world football has been embroiled in a storm following a much-criticised and ultimately abandoned plan to open the World Cup to private investment.
The 56-year-old Italian-Swiss lawyer, who has been in office since 2016, declined to answer a question from an AFP news agency journalist about whether he considered FIFA’s woes to be over.
Later, while attending a children’s football festival at a sports complex in Cali, he spoke of his “happiness” at being at the event.
“It is a joy to be here today,” the FIFA boss told dozens of children kitted out in football gear.
“Football is joy, football is happiness, football is unity”, he said, adding that “so many champions” were born “in this part of the world, in this part of Colombia”.
CONMEBOL throws backing behind Infantino
Infantino, who will seek a fourth and final term in the FIFA presidential election in Rabat next March, is facing criticism, notably from European body UEFA, which on Thursday maintained its threat to boycott the World Cup despite FIFA’s withdrawal of the private investment proposal.
CONMEBOL, which has only 10 FIFA-affiliated members but includes iconic federations such as Argentina and Brazil, had on Thursday expressed its “concern regarding the repeated unilateral actions taken” by FIFA.
However, when asked by a Colombian media outlet on Friday, the CONMEBOL president stated that “one cannot ignore the great work” done by Infantino.
“We must continue working for football through dialogue; it is not necessary to always agree,” Dominguez said.
After the powerful Argentine Football Association (AFA) and the Paraguayan federation pledged their backing on Thursday, Infantino also received support on Friday from two other South American federations – Venezuela’s and Ecuador’s.
In line with their confederation’s statement, they welcomed the withdrawal of the controversial plan to create a commercial entity, known as the FIFA Forward Enterprise, open to private investors.
In a letter to the FIFA chief, Ecuadorian federation president Francisco Egas Larreategui added that he had confidence in Infantino, “as well as in those currently leading football to continue working for the good of our sport”.
Close to figures on the right of politics, such as US President Donald Trump, Infantino attended de la Espriella’s presidential inauguration ceremony later on Friday.
Colombia’s incoming leader has broken with tradition by choosing to hold the ceremony in Cali, considered the capital of salsa, rather than before Congress in Bogota.

Flights serving eastern China were disrupted on Saturday as Typhoon Dolphin approached the coast, with some services cancelled and airlines offering flexible rebooking and refund options for affected passengers.
Most of the typhoon-related flight disruptions have been reported at airports in the cities of Ningbo, Wenzhou, Taizhou, Hangzhou and Shanghai, according to Chinese media.
Some travellers also reported receiving notifications that flights to and from Shanghai on Sunday and Monday would be cancelled, and shared concerns about possible disruptions in other cities on social media.
Flight service app Umetrip showed that Shanghai Pudong International Airport had 937 scheduled departing flights on Saturday, with 130 delayed and 66 cancelled as of noon. Another 72 arriving flights had been cancelled.
Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport had 69 flights cancelled on Saturday, including 35 departures and 34 arrivals, according to Umetrip.
Zhejiang province and Shanghai will be in the storm’s “dangerous semicircle”, where stronger winds and heavier rainfall are expected, according to the National Meteorological Centre (NMC).

title: ‘I couldn’t breathe’: the deadly health burden of wildfire smoke
summary:
Scientists race to untangle complex links between exposure and mortality as fire weather grows more prevalent

It seemed even inside you could smell that burning.”

full_text:
A thousand kilometres from the infernos gorging on northern Ontario’s boreal forests, Erin O’Connor watched the sky above Canada’s biggest city turn an “almost post-apocalyptic” orange as it filled with light-scattering particles of soot and ash. Stepping outside the halls of Toronto General hospital, where air filters were keeping patients safe from the worst of the fumes, she was struck by a smell so strong it felt like standing by a campfire.
“It really hit you in the face as soon as you walked outside,” said O’Connor, who runs University Health Network’s emergency department and saw a rise in patients presenting with allergies and shortness of breath. “As the days progressed, it was like that everywhere. It seemed even inside you could smell that burning.”
Far more than the flames that have engulfed southern Europe and North America in recent weeks, it is the smoke that dominates the astonishing death toll from combusting nature. Thick with toxic gases that inflame the airways and tiny particulates that breach the lungs and ride the bloodstream to hit every organ in the body, fumes from landscape fires kill 1.5 million people each year, a study in the Lancet found in 2024 – more than floods, flames, storms and heat combined.
So damaging are the lung-scarring effects of charred plant matter that people far from the fires may still perish. The plumes spewed by wildfires in Canada in 2023 caused 82,000 early deaths, a study in Nature found last year, with unfavourable winds pushing a third of the mortality burden into the US and another quarter into Europe. About 10% of the UK’s fine particulate pollution (PM2.5) comes from biomass burned abroad, researchers found in March.
Yet while scientists agree the health burden of wildfire smoke is jaw droppingly large, they are only beginning to untangle the complex links between exposure and mortality. The open research questions are growing more pressing as climate breakdown makes fire weather more severe. What if hotter infernos cause pollution to peak at even more extreme levels? What if bad air lasts several days or weeks? What if a severe episode hits before a person has fully recovered from the last bout of smoke?
Whims of the wind
The lack of answers in the existing research makes it hard to get a handle on how brutal the fallout from this furious fire season will be. Early signs are troubling, with vast tracts of vegetation torched close to big European cities and, after a late but explosive start to the North American fire season, smoke choking major population centres such as Chicago and New York City. In Toronto, which briefly had the worst air quality of any major metropolis in the world last month – a title claimed by Portland in the US on Wednesday – O’Connor said she could not remember the pollution ever having been so bad, with such a sudden onset that took so long to clear up.
“I had never looked outside and had the sky seem orange in the middle of the day,” said O’Connor, who amid treating patients and fielding media requests rushed to pull her son from summer camp. “Certainly, we have had other wildfire smoke, but in more of a transient way.”
Perhaps surprisingly, the death toll from a fire season can depend on the whims of the wind as much as the size of the fire. Wildfires in France spewed record amounts of pollution in the first half of the year and in Spain emissions have so far fallen just shy of the worst it has known. But even though monster infernos were halted alarmingly close to Madrid and Bordeaux, the smoke was mostly blown away from where people live. Daily particulate pollution levels still worsened across southern Europe and peaked at a staggering 342 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic metre (μg/m³) in Bordeaux on 24 July – and 486 μg/m³ in Limoges, 180km (112 miles) away, the following day – but other big cities in southern Europe were spared the extremes that doctors fear.
North America has not been so lucky. As winds blew south and south-east from scarcely populated forests in Ontario and the Northwest Territories, at least 36 million people across the continent were breathing air fouled by “very unhealthy” concentrations of PM2.5 that exceeded 125.5μg/m³ on 16 July, preliminary analysis conducted for the Guardian shows. At least 10 million people were exposed to more than 250μg/m³, according to the estimates, a level of daily pollution that smog-choked New Delhi saw no more than eight times last year.
Scientists say the hit to air quality in some big cities is reminiscent of the megafires in 2023 that came with vast death tolls. “As soon as we have massive population centres exposed, we’re going to see those increases,” said Stephanie Cleland, a wildfire health scientist at Simon Fraser University, who considered only people living within 25km of a measuring station in her calculations for the Guardian and said the figures are therefore conservative. “I would be concerned by the fact that it’s only been three years since this last happened and now we’re having it again.”
‘It felt like working in a war zone’
In a quiet suburb of Duluth, in north-east Minnesota, the worst of the smoke was seen, smelled and tasted on 16 July. Jae Jeon and Dan McClelland, a married couple who grow flowers for weddings and subscription deliveries, were looking forward to opening the windows after days baking in oppressive heat. Instead, they woke up to a fog that they soon realised was made up of something much worse. By late morning, their local hardware store had sold out of masks and air purifiers. People resorted to attaching furnace filters to box fans instead.
The McClellands were among 12,000 people in west Duluth exposed to an average of 541μg/m³ of fine particulate pollution, the analysis shows, higher than anywhere else in North America. They sent their sole farmworker home early after she complained of a headache but, with two weddings coming up on the weekend and little chance of cancellation, they still had plenty of flowers to pick and arrange. The couple got to work harvesting roses, yarrows, clematises and sweet peas, surrounded by a dystopian haze the likes of which they had never experienced.
“It felt like working in a war zone,” said Jae Jeon. “When I went outside, I couldn’t breathe, so I had to wear a mask, but it was still painful. After just a couple of minutes you started to get a headache.”
Climate breakdown made last month’s fire weather twice as likely in Canada and France, and 20 times more likely in Spain, recent rapid analyses have found, the result of planet-heating emissions that have made it easier for vegetation to dry out. As plants and trees combust, they spew a host of harmful particles that also trigger damaging inflammatory responses as the body seeks to purge foreign objects.
Scientists have relied on general air pollution relations to model the smoke’s chronic health effects, which make up the bulk of the death toll, because they lack long-term studies specific to wildfires. “The reason we don’t have them for wildfire smoke is because we haven’t had to deal with this as kind of a repeated ongoing problem,” said Michael Brauer, a wildfire health scientist at the University of British Columbia and co-author of the study on Canada’s 2023 fires. He first experienced wildfire smoke when he was about 40 years old, he said, while a 10-year-old child where he lives in British Columbia would have breathed it every summer of their life.
Compounding climate events
But the analogy to regular pollution is imperfect. Compared with other sources of PM2.5, such as factories or cars, wildfire smoke contains a greater share of organic compounds that increase inflammation and a higher concentration of ultra-fine particles that penetrate the deepest recesses of the lungs. title: Nitecore’s latest power bank is the lightest and most compact yet
summary: There's two things you should know about me, your intrepid reviewer: I hate the feature creep associated with modern power banks, and I love shaving grams off the gear I carry when backpacking, bikepacking, and trail running. So imagine my delight when Nitecore released a new generation of its ultralight NB10000 battery. After a few […]
full_text:
There’s two things you should know about me, your intrepid reviewer: I hate the feature creep associated with modern power banks, and I love shaving grams off the gear I carry when backpacking, bikepacking, and trail running. So imagine my delight when Nitecore released a new generation of its ultralight NB10000 battery. After a few weeks with it I can confidently say: Haribo be damned!
Nitecore’s latest power bank is the lightest and most compact yet
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The $83.95 NB10000 Gen 4 weighs just 146 grams, according to my scale, and measures 1.45 x 11.6 x 4.68cm (0.57 x 4.57 x 1.84 inches), according to Nitecore’s spec sheet. That makes it the lightest and most compact 10,000mAh power bank I can find. Even when factoring in the extra 6 grams added by the included USB-C lanyard, it still beats the previous ultralight champ: Nitecore’s NB10000 Gen 3.
As small as it is, the Gen 4’s 39Wh battery still fully recharged my aging iPhone 15 Pro twice, with a few watt-hours left in the tank. And with up to 22.5W of output, it can even top-up my 14-inch MacBook Pro when needed. It also supports pass-through to charge your gadgets as the power bank itself charges.
Have I found power bank perfection? Almost.
The Good
- Class-leading energy density
- Smallest and lightest 10,000mAh around
- Great for endurance athletes and backpackers
- Impressive water resistance
The Bad
- Expensive
- Knock-to-wake is hit-or-miss
- Silly RGB lighting
I like that the NB10000 Gen 4 gets all the basics right. It has a simple, four-element indicator to show the battery level, which I much prefer over a fancy display. It’s constructed out of carbon fiber sheets and offers IPX7 protection against water ingress, allowing it to withstand rain or even temporary submersion – exactly what you want from an adventure battery.
In my testing, I measured 33.58Wh of the claimed 39Wh capacity for an 86.1 percent efficiency. That’s a pretty good result for a premium power bank and a slight improvement on the 33.33Wh we measured on the Gen 3 model. That gives the Gen 4 an energy density of 229.98Wh/kg or 220.90Wh/kg with the cable — class-leading results, either way. The NB10000 Gen 4 supports PD, QC3.0, and Huawei’s SCP charging protocols.
The Gen 4 model also didn’t suffer from the overheating and shutdown issues we saw when the Gen 3 would run low on juice. I did, however, see a temporary interruption in power delivery when the Gen 4 unit was almost fully depleted, but that’s only because I had a meter attached — otherwise I wouldn’t have known since it continued charging almost immediately.
The only thing that could be considered superfluous is the animated RGB lighting that flows around the dual USB-C ports. The lights are there to guide you to the USB-C ports in a dark tent, says Nitecore, but you can also… feel them. Give the battery a double-knock near the top and the lights (and battery indicator) illuminate. This can be helpful if wearing gloves since Nitecore inexplicably opted for a touch-sensitive wake button on the Gen 4. Fortunately, that so-called “Touch Button” did reliably sense my wet finger in testing. The knock-to-wake feature seemed to only work about 75 percent of the time, but it, and the RGB lights, can be disabled if you want.
The lights will also glow yellow (regular mode) or green (eco) after a long press of the power button if you want to toggle between full power and extended life, respectively. Eco mode works by dropping the output to a slow 5W (5V at 1A) max. This can keep the power bank from automatically shutting off when charging low-draw devices like headlamps, watches, or wireless earbuds. It can also yield a little more total charge capacity by producing less heat waste, and allow the battery to operate closer to its native voltage resulting in less conversion loss.
The Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 is the ideal power bank for endurance athletes, backpackers, or anyone looking for an ultralight and ultracompact power bank that mostly avoids feature creep. The only real negative is the price, having gone up to $83.95 since the launch of the $64.95 Gen 3 model two years ago. That makes the Gen 4 power bank two to three times more expensive than the typical 10,000mAh power bank, but it can save you 50 grams or more. That’s a price premium I can see lots of active, outdoorsy people happily paying for.
All photos by Thomas Ricker / The Verge

title: Another Bitcoin infrastructure exploit hits, this time draining Lightning payment servers
full_text:
Another Bitcoin infrastructure exploit hits, this time draining Lightning payment servers
BTCPay told users running LND to update immediately or take servers offline after attackers stole credentials that can control Lightning wallets and move funds.
- Attackers exploited a critical vulnerability in BTCPay Server to steal funds from Lightning nodes running LND, prompting urgent calls to update to version 2.4.2 or take servers offline.
- The flaw allowed unauthenticated access to LND “.macaroon” credential files, enabling attackers to seize control of affected Lightning nodes and drain their channels, though BTCPay’s standard on-chain wallets were not impacted.
- Victims including hardware-wallet maker Foundation and bitcoin publication Citadel21 reported their Lightning nodes were swept, as BTCPay and the Bitcoin Red Team investigate and prepare a full postmortem on the incident.
A rough week for bitcoin's software is getting worse, this time hitting merchants who accept bitcoin 
Attackers drained Lightning nodes running behind BTCPay Server late on Friday after exploiting a critical vulnerability that exposed the credentials protecting them, the team said in an X post.
BTCPay confirmed funds were stolen and told anyone running LND, the most widely used software for operating a Lightning node, to update immediately to version 2.4.2 or take the server offline.
The project has not disclosed how many users were hit or how much bitcoin was taken.
The flaw allowed an unauthenticated remote attacker to obtain “.macaroon” files, or credentials that give software permission to interact with an LND Lightning node. BTCPay said the attacks it reviewed targeted those files, which could then be used to take control of the node and move funds.
Hardware-wallet maker Foundation was among the victims. Chief Executive Zach Herbert said attackers drained the company's BTCPay Lightning node overnight, closing its channels and sweeping the funds. Its BTCPay on-chain hot wallet was untouched.
Citadel21, the bitcoin publication run by pseudonymous commentator hodlonaut, also reported that its Lightning node had been swept, though it said little money was held there.
The vulnerability had already been reported to BTCPay by members of the Bitcoin Red Team — a group of developers that began pointing AI models at bitcoin codebases this week and has filed thousands of findings across hundreds of projects since.
Read More: Bitcoin developers flag 85 critical bugs in an "extremely bad" situation.
BTCPay credited Red Team members Craig Raw, Rob Hamilton, Calle and Evan Kaloudis with responsibly disclosing the issue and helping analyze it.
The group's stated reason for publishing findings quickly was that people outside it would arrive at the same bugs, and by the time BTCPay's public warning went out, attackers were already exploiting this one against live servers.
Meanwhile, BTCPay narrowed the scope after its initial alert, saying its standard on-chain wallets, including hot wallets generated inside BTCPay, are not affected by the credential flaw.
The exposure applies specifically to deployments using LND, and funds held inside LND's own on-chain wallet can still be at risk because they sit under the compromised Lightning node.
BTCPay has not yet published technical details of the vulnerability, saying operators need time to patch. A full postmortem is due in the coming days.

summary: 在實體零售業普遍面臨數位化衝擊的今天，「縮減門市」往往意味著業務收縮或衰退。然而，日本知名連鎖零售巨頭 GEO […]
full_text:
在實體零售業普遍面臨數位化衝擊的今天，「縮減門市」往往意味著業務收縮或衰退。然而，日本知名連鎖零售巨頭 GEO（ゲオ）近期在懷舊遊戲（Retro Games）市場的神操作，卻展現一個令人震撼的反直覺現象：銷售門市從過去的近 1,000 家銳減至僅剩約 99 家（規模縮減至十分之一），其懷舊遊戲的銷售額卻反而成長至停售前的 1.3 至 1.4 倍。
這個舊遊戲「起死回生」的奇蹟，背後隱含著當代消費文化的重要轉變──對現代人而言，特別是年輕世代，「懷舊」早已不再只是重溫過去，而是一種前所未有的「新鮮感」。
沒經歷過，反而成了最新鮮的體驗
過去，業界普遍認為購買紅白機（FC）、超級任天堂（SFC）或初代 PlayStation 遊戲的主力族群，必然是那些想要「重拾童年回憶」的中年消費者。然而 GEO 的市場調查揭示了一個關鍵轉變：越來越多根本沒經歷過 80、90 年代家用主機盛世的年輕玩家，開始熱衷於購買並遊玩這些懷舊卡帶與主機。
這種現象並非遊戲業獨有。從 2010 年代起黑膠唱片的逆勢復甦（日本黑膠產量從 2009 年低谷的 10 萬張飆升至 2025 年的 337 萬張），到近年底片相機（CCD／底片相機）在青年族群中的流行，都驗證了同一個邏輯：在高度數位化且標準化的現代生活裡，帶有實體觸感、像素點陣風格與獨特限制感的舊時代產物，對年輕人來說具備極高的神秘感與探索樂趣。
透過 YouTube 遊戲開箱影片、社群媒體的傳播，以及二手交易平台（C2C）的熱絡，舊遊戲擺脫了「過時」的標籤，被賦予了全新的流行文化意涵。年輕人拿著橘色的〈瑪利歐兄弟〉卡帶讚嘆「原來最初的瑪利歐長這樣」，這種探索未知的興奮感，與長輩的懷舊情緒截然不同，卻創造了更具爆發力的消費推動力。
海外懷舊熱從未熄滅：廠商推舊作重製版，令當年熱潮再現
除了年輕世代的認知轉變、遊戲廠商對舊遊戲的重視，外部環境也對日本懷舊遊戲事業起到積極作用。近年遊戲大廠頻繁推出經典遊戲作品的 Remake（重製版）或 Remaster（高畫質復刻版）。當新世代玩家體驗完新版後，社群上便會掀起「當年原作究竟長怎樣？」的討論熱潮，進而回流至實體二手市場尋找初代作品。
而隨著入境旅遊強勁復甦，大量外國遊客將日本二手遊戲店視為尋寶聖地。對於外國玩家而言，保留完好的日本原版遊戲卡帶與包裝，不只是遊戲，更是具備高度收藏價值與紀念意義的文化工藝品，訪日觀光客的「文化聖地巡禮」為產業推波助瀾。
精準零售策略：發展舊遊戲「尋寶體驗」
當然單單只有市場需求還不夠，GEO 能在門市數量減少 90% 的情況下實現營業額大幅成長，歸功於其精準的商業經營轉型。
▲ GEO 埼玉縣北越谷門市。（Source：GEO）
「全國回收，集中銷售」資源集中效應 GEO 透過全國超過 900 家門市（正在販售全新遊戲的門市）進行懷舊遊戲收購，再集中分配至全日本精選的 99 家旗艦及客流密集門市銷售。這種運作模式讓單一門市的庫存豐富度大幅提升，確保顧客每次造訪都有新發現。
製造「尋寶」樂趣
GEO 放棄了過去按機種嚴格分類的沉悶擺設，改採類似「唐吉訶德」（DON DON DONKI）的密集陳列風格。透明塑膠袋裝著無盒卡帶掛滿牆面、掌上型主機放置於精美展示櫃、大型主機則堆疊於架下。這種看似略帶雜亂卻驚喜連連的空間設計，大幅拉長了顧客在店內的停留時間，進一步誘發了衝動消費與「尋寶」（お宝探し）的快感。
結語：數位浪潮下，實體體驗再次被人珍惜
隨著 Sony 宣布將於 2028 年起逐步淘汰 PlayStation 主機的實體光碟、全面轉向數位下載，實體媒介的生存空間無疑將進一步被壓縮。然而，正是因為「數位下載」缺乏觸感與實體空間的陪伴感，實體卡帶、紙本說明書與盒裝封面所承載的「回憶價值」與「物質質感」才顯得越發珍貴。
GEO 的成功轉型給予了實體零售業深刻的啟示：縮小規模不代表退縮，而是將重點項目聚焦。當「舊東西」被賦予了「新體驗」，「懷舊」物品不再是老舊無用的古董，而是將舊有文化向下個世代傳遞的橋樑。只要新一代玩家依然會為了親手拿到一塊數十年前的遊戲卡帶而感到驚喜，這份跨越時代的新鮮感，就將繼續為實體門市注入生生不息的生命力。

title: Hundreds stranded on second day of disruption at Bristol Airport
summary: Flights are restarting with delays and diversions after 14 hours of cancellations.
full_text:
Airport disruption a 'shambles' as flights restart
- Published
Disruption because of a runway defect at Bristol Airport continues, as flights start to depart.
Hundreds of passengers were stranded on Friday evening after the decision was made to close the runway shortly after 18:00 BST. All flights were suspended until 08:00 on Saturday.
Flights have since restarted amid delayed take offs and diversions.
In a short statement on the airport website, a spokesperson said: "There will be some disruption to some flights today. We apologise for any inconvenience caused."
More from Bristol
- Late night flights suspended due to runway defect 
  - Published12 hours ago
- Charges dropped in racially-aggravated assault case 
  - Published15 hours ago
Anyone caught up in the disruption should contact their airline, they added.
No further official information about the nature of the defect has been released.
A number of people spoke to the BBC on Friday evening about their experience at the airport - among them Paul Smith, who was due to fly to Glasgow for his son's 20th birthday but had to cancel his trip.
"The communication, advice and support for passengers has been really poor," he said.
There were no announcements on the tannoy system for over an hour, he said, which meant EasyJet reps in the departure lounge were the only source of information.
"What we've heard is that there's a hole in the runway."
Dave Blackwell, travelling home from Rhodes in Greece, said it had been "a shambles" since his flight back to Bristol was diverted to Newcastle.
"We were in Rhodes Airport for three hours with no information. Now we have all been told our flight is going to Newcastle and then a five or six hour bus ride - why Newcastle? How appalling," he said.

title: Farage and Tice sue NCA over alleged leaks of financial information
summary: The Reform leaders claim the National Crime Agency supplied details about party donations to the media.
full_text:
Farage and Tice sue NCA over alleged leaks of financial information
- Published
Richard Tice has said he and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage are suing the National Crime Agency (NCA) over the alleged leaking of confidential financial information.
The Boston and Skegness MP and Reform deputy leader told Talk TV they believed the NCA had committed "multiple criminal offences" and said they would be seeking an apology and damages.
He accused them of leaking "individual bank statements, bank transfers, details of conversations with bank managers from different banks".
Last month Tice wrote to the agency to ask if they would investigate whether they were responsible for the leaking of private financial information to the media.
It followed reports that payments made to his company Britain Means Business by the mother of the convicted fraudster George Cottrell were flagged to the NCA as part of its suspicious activity reports (SARs) programme, which alerts law enforcement to potential instances of money laundering.
SARs are not crime reports.
Tice said at the time he only became aware of it when contacted by the Guardian newspaper, which broke the story.
The NCA has been carrying out an internal investigation but Tice told Talk TV it was "playing for time and we've said we're done with it".
A Reform UK spokesperson said claims had been filed at the High Court. BBC News has not seen the detail of the claims.
A spokesperson for the NCA said: "Following complaints brought by Richard Tice MP and Nigel Farage, the NCA's Professional Standards Unit is conducting an investigation. That work is ongoing. It would not be appropriate to comment further at this time."
As first reported by the Telegraph, Tice's company Tisun Investment received a loan of £80,000 from Cottrell in late 2024.
That same year, Britain Means Business received a £1m donation from Cotrell's mother.
Data from the Electoral Commission shows that Britain Means Business donated £500,000 to Reform UK in the same month.
These payments were flagged to the NCA as part of the SARs programme.
Cottrell's relationship with Reform has been under scrutiny in recent months after the Sunday Times reported he had supplied Farage with support including security and social media staff in the year before he became an MP.
Under parliamentary rules, newly elected MPs have to declare gifts or benefits received in the 12 months before their election that relate to their "parliamentary or political activities".
However, there is an exemption for gifts and benefits that are "purely personal".
Reform has argued that Farage did not breach the guidelines by not declaring the support from Cottrell because the support was provided in a "purely personal capacity".
