title: Israel accused of weaponising archaeology at ancient West Bank sites
summary: Israel is planning large-scale land expropriations in historic, Palestinian areas of the West Bank.
full_text:
Israel accused of weaponising archaeology at ancient West Bank sites
- Published
Up in the hills above the Roman columns of the ancient site of Sebastia, in the occupied West Bank, are olive fields that have been cultivated for generations by Palestinian families.
One of the landowners, Abu Mudif, says he has received notification that his land is part of a tranche of about 450 acres that the Israeli authorities are taking possession of in order, they say, to protect and develop the site for a major new national park.
Typically, Palestinian landowners receive little or no payment for such land expropriation. And even when it is offered, most refuse it as they see accepting it as giving recognition and legitimacy to the loss of what they see as their patrimony.
It's a vital income for Abu Mudif to lose of course, but it goes deeper than that for him.
"If I wanted to describe it, the closest description I can give is that it is like having your soul ripped away. I cannot imagine myself without my land."
Nahed Sakha owns a local restaurant that is under threat of demolition.
He says the Israeli plan seems to be to cut Palestinian residents off from the archaeological site, which dates back thousands of years and has significant remains from the ancient Jewish past, as well as many other eras including the Romans, the Crusaders and the Ottomans.
"Restoration work has now begun along with excavations," he says. "Landowners were told that no-one would be allowed to use or plough their land."
The concerns of the village that surrounds Sebastia have been echoed by the United Nations culture and education agency, Unesco, which has now declared it not just a World Heritage Site but also added it to the List of World Heritage in Danger.
Unesco says that the main threat facing the site concerns what it calls the "planned expropriation and creation of the 'Samaria' (Shomron) national park, which could divide the property".
Standing on a path between the entrance car park in Sebastia on one side - where the Roman-era forum once stood - and the columns of the basilica on the other, the village mayor, Mohammed Azem, looks down to his right at some rubbish left in the ruins.
He says locals are now worried about reaching down to clean the area as it might cause problems with Israeli security forces and settlers.
The path on which he stands divides the site between Area B of the West Bank - which is under Palestinian civil and Israeli security control - and Area C, which is under full Israeli civil and security control.
Last week, Israel allocated roughly 113 million shekels (£27.8m), external to expanding its control over archaeological sites in the West Bank. Some projects involve sites in areas administered by the Palestinian Authority.
In the remains of the Roman theatre, Israeli activist Alon Arad - who heads Emek Shaveh, an Israeli group that aims to ensure that the ancient heritage of the region belongs to all communities - says that the Israeli authorities have bypassed consultation with the local administration and residents of Sebastia.
"The thing is that Israel is not the owner of this place. This is a Palestinian heritage site. And in order to develop it in a positive way, it has to be done with the local community, with the municipality, so they can benefit."
The Israeli plans would see Sebastia's entrance moved to the other side of the vast site, away from the village and current car park and shops.
The Palestinian tourism and foreign ministries have expressed their hope that recognition by Unesco may buttress international support for their opposition to Israeli land seizures in Sebastia.
But the Israeli Foreign Minister, Gideon Saar, has portrayed Unesco's move as enabling Palestinian efforts to diminish historic Jewish ties to the West Bank.
"No vote in an international organisation can change history," he asserted.
Further to the south in the West Bank and just in sight of Jerusalem is Herodium, a manmade hill with an extraordinary palace built on its summit by King Herod, who ruled the Kingdom of Judea just before the Christian era.
Recently here, too, Israel has begun to expropriate land - this time about 80 acres - for what it says is the "preservation and development" of the site.
Peace Now - an Israeli organisation that monitors settlements - says: "Under international law, as well as according to rulings of the Israeli Supreme Court, Israel is prohibited from expropriating land for settlement purposes or exclusively for the benefit of Israeli citizens".
"Consequently, in order for the expropriation to be considered lawful, the state will likely argue that the site is intended to serve both Palestinian and Israeli populations, despite the apparent fact that its primary rationale and purpose are linked to settlement expansion and Israeli control."
For Shmuel Browns, who has worked on excavations in Herodium and leads deeply enthused guided tours, it's vital for Israeli archaeologists and officials to be able to oversee and protect places that are so freighted with historical and religious significance.
"Israel feels responsible to look after the archaeology, the artifacts, the history of this land," he says.
But there has also been a drive to go further than this among far-right members of Israel's current government.
A new law was proposed earlier this year that would have transferred control of archaeological sites to the Israeli heritage ministry from the Civil Administration, which operates under military authority, and given it sweeping powers to seize land for archaeological preservation across the West Bank.
That bill passed its first reading in parliament in May but is now on hold as elections are coming up. It may never re-emerge.
Back in Sebastia, the Israeli activist Alon Arad says the very fact that the bill was put forward shows how archaeology itself has been weaponised in the West Bank.
"This is exactly how the mechanism works. You use archaeology, you use it in order to do excavations and to the narrative, to rewrite history, but you also use it in order to allocate lands or reallocate lands from Palestinian to Israeli," he warns.
Increasingly, Palestinian residents of Sebastia fear that their close connection with the ruins is in danger of being lost.

title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
summary: The country is home to some of the world's most unique species - but it is losing them at an alarming rate.
full_text:
Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
- Published
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.
Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.
Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.
Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland – in the south-western corner of Australia – is one of the few places they remain.
As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.
Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.
This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.
Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.
Australia has long been celebrated as a nature haven, home to some of the world's most unique plant and animal species. More than 80% cannot be found anywhere else.
But it has arguably become the extinction capital of the world, losing roughly four species every decade - and the decline is only worsening.
Dedicated volunteers and under-funded conservationists have been slowing the army of increasing threats, but experts fear that without urgent action and political courage, the biodiversity Australia says it loves is headed for a bloodbath.
"It's not even a case of imagining it, it's happening in front of our own eyes," Professor Euan Ritchie tells the BBC.
The many threats driving extinction
If spotting a rare creature in the wild wasn't challenging enough, the numbat is a squirrel-sized camouflage connoisseur, explains Dr Tony Friend, the godfather of conservation in the state of Western Australia.
"They just slept in today," jokes Rob McLean, president of the Numbat Taskforce, a volunteer group which makes a lot of Tony's thinly-resourced work possible.
For two weeks each spring, as the young start venturing from their burrows, this team drives a daily circuit and records every numbat spotted. They log GPS coordinates, measure the distance to the road, and use a complicated equation to estimate the density of the animals in these woods and, from that, broader population health.
One person sits in concentrated silence at each window, another perched in the back of the pick-up truck, ducking for the occasional limb branching from trees which rise around us.
Through the trunks, we get the occasional glimpse of the razed farmland which tightly fences this pocket of protected woodland. On the side of one trail is a machine which detects and sprays feral cats and foxes with poison, another reminder of the perils numbats face.
"This year's been a bit of a feast," Rob admits.
For hours on end, we cruise around, seeing parrots, wallabies, a goanna and a couple of echidnas - but no numbats.
Tony arrived at Dryandra back in the 80s to find a numbat population fewer than 50. Many of the culprits then were the same as those still driving extinctions across the nation today.
Swathes of critical habitat are being cleared for development or industries like farming, mining and timber.
Leaving a trail of destruction in their wake are introduced pests: fire ants, cane toads, rabbits, foxes, feral cats.
Invasive weeds like lantana are choking the Australian bush, chlamydia has sent koalas to the edge of existence across much of the country, while the skin-eating chytrid fungus has caused seven frog extinctions here and counting.
The changing climate is creating unliveable conditions for some species, like native flying foxes which are dropping out of trees in their thousands due to extreme temperatures.
For others it is eliminating their food or their homes.
Climate change is also driving natural disasters which fry and drown both plants and animals with now frightening regularity.
The infamous Black Summer bushfires of 2019-20, for example, killed an estimated three billion animals. The successive years of record-breaking flooding which followed were so widespread it's impossible to estimate the impact on wildlife.
Many species once abundant across the continent are now isolated to increasingly small and disjointed patches, each impact compounding and leaving them more vulnerable to the next.
There are small, yet determined, efforts to slow the momentum of decline.
As a young numbat scoffs his breakfast – custard with "termite sprinkles" – at Perth Zoo, a keeper explains how this stud's upcoming release at Dryandra will help boost genetic diversity.
"When you get that feedback: your babies have got babies, it's very satisfying," Vicki Power says.
Breeding programmes like this have also made setting up additional populations of an array of threatened species possible.
But many cannot survive in the true wild, where large-scale predator control remains an endless battle, and are instead sent to fenced nature reserves, themselves high-maintenance undertakings facing problems like in-breeding and overpopulation.
Habitat protection or restoration projects have been ramping up, but they are not keeping pace with destruction, particularly in the most critical areas.
Scientists are also trying to fight disease, though that's an expensive and laborious endeavour, which for most species buys only a little more time. Others are preserving genetic material in case we ever work out how to resurrect species from the dead.
A hundred species lost - and counting
Scientists agree that we're living though the world's sixth mass extinction event, the first caused by humans. But Australia is at the front of this trend.
It leads the world in mammal extinctions, and medals when it comes to the loss of other species classes too.
"Despite Australia being one of the wealthiest countries per capita in the world and having more than its fair share of world-leading scientists… we have a truly awful record of conserving species," Ritchie says.
"And things aren't getting better."
The Australian government's official extinctions list sits at 67, but researchers are confident at least 100 plant and animal species have been lost forever.
They suspect the true figure is far higher. The country is still discovering species which have already been wiped out.
Though the rate of extinction in Australia has stayed stable, at around four per decade, the number of threatened species is still climbing quickly, and the deterioration of many is only gathering speed.
This trajectory has some scary flow-on effects, experts warn. Australia's biodiversity "underpins everything", ecologist Jack Pascoe says.
Think food production, tourism, construction – much of the economy. Potential scientific breakthroughs could be stymied: in medicine, agriculture and even climate change adaptation. And for First Nations Australians, the decline also threatens their culture.
"We think of ourselves as custodians of all life on Earth… so there's a much more personal and social feeling of loss that comes when these things are not doing well or we lose them forever," Pascoe, a man from the Yuin Aboriginal nation, says.
Decades of failures
Though environment protection is a state responsibility, the federal government oversees matters of national importance.
Labor took office in 2022, promising no new extinctions under its watch, and it has sought to make nature protection a defining feature of its second term.

title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
summary: The former Old Vic landlady Linda Carter is set to leave Walford.
full_text:
Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
- Published
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.
She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.
Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.
Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".
The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.
Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".
Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.
More than 7m people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assualt led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.
In 2022, Linda Carter's husband vanished into the sea trying to save Janine Butcher. The soap followed her as she grieved and began to navigate life as a single mother.
She was also at the centre of the 2023 Christmas Day episode where she stabbed Keanu Taylor to death to save the life of her friend Sharon Watts, played by Letitia Dean.
More recently, the character opened a B&B and had several romances.
"I will miss my friends and colleagues hugely, but I am looking forward to my next chapter and spending more time with my wonderful boys," Bright said, referring to her husband and three sons.
Bright appeared on Strictly Come Dancing in 2015, and has starred in films including Ali G Indahouse in 2002 and 2005's Kinky Boots.

title: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
summary: TikTok creator Zainab Jiwa seems to be giving Hollywood A-listers on the red carpet a run for their money.
full_text:
Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
- Published
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"
This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.
The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.
She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.
"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.
"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."
"I’m still in shock,” she adds. “The thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."
The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.
While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" – where stars match outfits to a film's themes – Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.
Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.
"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.”
Arriving for our interview at BBC Broadcasting House this week, her look was on-point in an olive shirt, tie, and brooches. "I put in effort today," she says.
She's a self-confessed fashion addict. "From the womb," she says, when I ask her when her passion started.
Her other love is film - but she initially kept that as a hobby. Still, she posted videos on social media for fun about her favourite films and outfits inspired by them.
Soon, major studios took notice. Disney was first, offering her a junket interview for the series Moon Knight, where she got to interview stars on the red carpet.
"I thought it was a scam,” she says. “I can’t watch that back. I was NOT good.”
Today, Zainab is a full-time creator and presenter, interviewing A-listers like Denzel Washington, Paul Mescal and Tom Hiddleston – while decked head to toe in outfits paying homage to the films.
She's one of many digital content creators on the red carpet, with others including Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg, Reece Feldman and social media personality Jake Shane.
It's not always easy. Sometimes, Zainab gets invites to premieres the night before, meaning a mad rush to sort her look before travelling to the event - often by public transport (“and I look ridiculous”).
She works with a range of designers and brands, but says she also keeps costs down by reusing items as much as possible.
Her outfits are purposely bold, allowing her to "break the ice" with stars. For House of the Dragon season two, she wore a red gown by a student designer featuring three faces wearing hijabs.
"I'm a bit extra, but I like to add culture in everything I do," she says.
For Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she customised her look with spiderweb henna. For Gladiator II, she wore gold armour.
She admits she has worried whether dressing modestly will make it harder for her to succeed in this industry, but she finds pleasure in it too.
"I have a fun time working around the fact that I cover my hair or I cover my arms," she says. "I'd call it halalify the look. I'd always say, ‘'but how do I halalify this?'"
"I enjoy that bit the most because it shows there's no restriction really here."
But while Zainab spends much of her time rubbing shoulders with Hollywood royalty, home life in Harrow, north-west London is completely different.
"Oh my god, my house is chaos," she laughs. Storage space is at a premium, and outfits often end up "shoved somewhere".
She has a cat, siblings who often pop in, and parents who are frequently enlisted for wardrobe emergencies.
Despite it not being the career trajectory they’d expected for their daughter, Zainab says her parents are now "so supportive".
With 660,000 followers on TikTok and close to 400,000 on Instagram, she's becoming a key content creator in this field. But she also faces criticism - including from some who claim her outfits are not modest enough.
"There's always hate in this industry," she says.
But she adds: "For every negative comment, there's so many positive ones.
"If I'm doing it to inspire other people, or entertain other people, or educate other people, if that's still happening, then I really don't care about the rest."
For now though, Zainab is swept up in enjoying a string of blockbusters.
"The summer's felt good for film - I think it's exciting," she says.
"And there's loads more coming. We've got Dune. We've got Doomsday," she says.
"I love film and TV. I think it's a really fun way to build community," she adds. "I'm just a fan. At the end of the day, I'm just a fan."

title: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world
summary: For many, a total solar eclipse is a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for a dedicated few, it's a deep passion.
full_text:
What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world
- Published
On Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.
For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.
Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.
It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".
But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.
He's since filmed the northern lights numerous times - he goes to Iceland once a month and leads tour groups there - and has photographed various auroras, eclipses and bioluminescence.
But this is his first total solar eclipse.
"I kept wanting more," he says, and Europe's first total solar eclipse for more than 25 years is "like what the World Cup is to football" for enthusiasts like him.
"I'll be honest, it's like an addiction now," he tells me.
I'm speaking to him the day after he's finished his marathon drive from England, across France and into Spain. He only paused to take photos of the night sky and rest for a few hours in Bordeaux. "I'm quite sleep deprived."
The path of total eclipse begins at the tip of Siberia before curving round the Arctic Ocean and crossing parts of Greenland and Iceland.
It then proceeds across a stretch of the northern Atlantic Ocean before reaching northern Spain and finishing in the Mediterranean. Other parts of Europe will see a partial eclipse.
The total eclipse is only expected to last a couple of minutes for people who watch it, but that doesn't deter eclipse hunters from crossing continents to witness it.
Samantha Phillips-Brown and her husband Gregory have flown to Iceland and hired a camper van so they can drive to a remote area to see it.
This will be the second solar eclipse they've witnessed.
It was the awe-inspiring power of the first one they saw, near their home in upstate New York in 2023, that convinced them to travel for this one. They booked their flights and van more than a year ago.
"It was such a phenomenal experience to see the Sun start going dark and hear, suddenly, the birds stop chirping," recalls Samantha. "It's just a very strange experience."
Gregory thinks of how Iceland's first settlers must have felt witnessing such a phenomena more than a millennium ago, a time of mythological rather than scientific explanation.
"They really didn't know what was happening, didn't know how long it was going to last... it must have been quite terrifying for them, in a way."
They are spending the days before the eclipse driving round eastern parts of Iceland to go hiking and camping.
The path of totality crosses the western part of Iceland and they hope to find a spot in the Westfjords peninsula to witness it.
Although they've heard rumours of roads being closed to stop too many people overwhelming the area, so are keen to get there a couple of days before the spectacle.
Samantha, who her husband describes as an "obsessive travel planner", is all over the Facebook groups and social media pages being used by eclipse hunters to share information and advice.
She's expecting a good turnout given the number of eclipse glasses she's seen people with in Iceland. "They're really trying to prepare everybody," she says.
"What I expect, as we start inching westward, is we're going to see more and more of them."
Andrew Wills is also going to an island to see the eclipse, albeit a much warmer one: Majorca.
He's travelling with his wife and his dad, who is 90. Father and son witnessed Europe's last total solar eclipse together in 1999 while stood atop St Agnes Beacon in Cornwall.
The landmark, believed by some to be a Bronze Age bowl barrow, offers panoramic views across the Cornish countryside and out to the Atlantic. It was a cloudy day, remembers Andrew.
"We didn't see the shadow rushing across the sea towards us, though we did see the dawn appearing and it getting closer very quickly," he says. "It was awe-inspiring."
He has high hopes for a clearer day in Majorca where he has booked a villa near the town of Andraitx, located in the west of the island.
Andrew has earmarked a spot nearby he hopes will give a good view across the sea. Their location in the path of totality means the eclipse will likely happen low on the horizon.
"We're going to take a couple of camping chairs with us, so Dad can sit if we can get there an hour or so before."
The islands of Majorca and Menorca will be the last places on land to view the eclipse before the Sun sets and the shadow disappears.
Eclipses have fascinated Andrew ever since he saw his first in St Agnes all those years ago.
"We live on a planet where we have this amazing coincidence. Where the Sun is 400 times bigger than the moon but the moon is 400 times closer.
"And so when the moon passes in front of the Sun and between Earth, it casts this perfect shadow."
It made him appreciate the delicacy of life on our planet in the way astronomer Carl Sagan once did when speaking of the Pale Blue Dot photograph.
"We are tiny little specks in a huge vast area of nothingness," says Andrew. "We're amazingly lucky to be alive."

title: Your university clearing survival guide ahead of results day
summary: From listing your potential outcomes to picking up the phone, this is how to get the most out of clearing.
full_text:
Your university clearing survival guide ahead of results day
- Published
Have you changed your mind about the university course you want to start after getting your results?
Maybe did not apply to university originally but now want to go, or you might not end up getting the grades you need to make it into your firm choice.
If that is you, the clearing process will have you covered.
With results day rapidly approaching on Thursday 13 August, here is everything you need to know.
What is clearing?
Clearing is how universities and colleges fill any places that they still have on their courses and how students can change their course or place of study.
This year, clearing runs from 2 July to 19 October.
Prospective students can use clearing if:
- You are applying after 30 June
- You did not receive any offers (or none you wanted to accept)
- You did not meet the conditions on your offers
- You have declined your firm place using the "decline my place" button in your application
- You are not already holding any offer from a university or college, and the course still has places
- You want to go to your insurance choice instead of your firm. You will have to check in clearing whether your insurance choice will accept you
- You have done better than expected and want to go to a different university
What can students do ahead of results day?
Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing ahead of results day.
She suggests writing down all possible outcomes that you could get, and then finding alternatives to those outcomes.
For example, depending on available places:
- If I get AAA, then I could do physics at Sussex
- BBC could be physics at Aberystwyth
- CCD could be physics at Nottingham Trent
The Ucas website has a search tool to find courses, which you can find here, external. You can filter the options to the year of study, type of course and to those with clearing vacancies. It is the only official vacancy list, so it is the most up-to-date.
For those who are unsure about their course choice and want to change, Wade says it is important to talk to a trusted adviser first, like a family member or teacher.
She says students should think about why they chose that option in the first place, and why you might now be changing your mind.
She says she finds most of the people who go through clearing are those that are applying to university for the first time.
Haadi Nasir, a student at the University of Manchester, was one of those people.
At first, he wanted to take a gap year after his A-levels so did not apply for university, but was persuaded to go by family and friends after achieving "great grades".
On the day, with the help of his A-level teachers, he filled in a Ucas form, applied to six universities via clearing and picked the University of Manchester to study politics and modern history.
"The good thing about clearing is that you can apply to as many universities as you want, unlike with Ucas, where you are limited to five," he says.
"That was definitely stress-relieving," he says.
For those on the fence about university, Nasir recommends people put in a Ucas application "just in case" to avoid the stress of results day.
That's a piece of advice that is echoed by Wade.
"You will need a referee, which is why I'd suggest doing it now," she says.
"Let's say [you've] got to email the teacher, the teacher's got to add a reference, then Ucas only gets sent once all of those parts are sent together."
Nasir says he wished he was more prepared for clearing, and advises students to write down some notes on location, accommodation and cost for each university you contact.
"Make sure you know whether you qualify before calling," he says.
"With my university I was required to have a specific A-level, so make sure you meet the requirements."
How does it work and what do you need to do on results day?
Ucas updates at 08:00 on results day, so you can often find out whether you have been accepted to your firm choice before knowing your results.
But Wade advises holding off and waiting until you get your results before you open the Ucas website.
"I would say try and steer away from the temptation, get your results in hand and then look at your Ucas track, because then you can action that decision as opposed to having 90 minutes of freak-out."
Jamie Bradford, head of future students at Leicester De Montfort University, also says it is easier to start conversations about clearing with your results in hand.
On Ucas, before you add a clearing choice in your application, you need to contact the university or college and give them your clearing number - which you can find in your application - and personal ID, so they can find it.
"It's amazing how many students don't actually talk about the course or the place at all," says Bradford.
"All they want is just the offer - 'I've got these grades, can you take me?' - in reality, it's three or more years of your life. The university is a big decision."
Bradford says students need to ask about the day-to-day of the course, the campus and whether accommodation is available.
"Work up a priority list," he says.
"For us, it's about fitting the right student to the right course, not just about getting any offer."
Wade says students should go through a list of alternatives, and once they have received offers and discussed student finance with the universities, have a break to chat with a trusted person.
She also stresses that students need to have the confidence to pick up the phone and call universities.
"I know it feels scary, but you are the client, you do get to ask these questions," she says.
"You don't even need to ring this university to say, 'Can I get into this course, please?' You could say, 'Hey, what course could you offer me?' Because you know what, universities need these students."
Some universities, like Leicester De Montfort, also operate clearing through WhatsApp as well as via phone.
How long do you have to decide on an offer?
Bradford says many students "can't afford" to spend days ruminating on their offer as popular courses do get filled quickly, but it is important to not agree to one straight away.
"Spend a small amount of time thinking, what do I really want from my experience? Don't panic buy and accept the first offer that comes along."
Wade says students need to ask their preferred university how much time they have to accept the offer on results day as every university is different.
"The more super-selective the university, the less time they will have," she says.
"Generally, I would always say sleep on it. Most universities will give students some time, but ask that question on the phone."

title: Raw images, no filters: Why MySpace fans want it back as relaunch hinted
summary: Fans and creators say a revived MySpace must feel personal, not algorithm-driven.
full_text:
Raw images, no filters: Why MySpace fans want it back as relaunch hinted
- Published
For Monticah Hawkins, a 31-year-old real-estate agent in Atlanta, MySpace wasn't just a website – it was a ritual.
"You could be authentic on MySpace," she says. "Upload raw images, no filters. You could have snot coming out your nose and nobody would judge."
MySpace, once the world's biggest social network, is flirting with a comeback. Its owners, brothers Tim and Chris Vanderhook, say they plan to relaunch the platform, though no date or product details have been announced.
A spokesperson for Viant, which owns MySpace, says the company does not have any updates to share "at this time."
But just the idea of a comeback has stirred nostalgia among people who remember the MySpace days of more than 20 years ago as a place where personal pages were messy, loud, and deeply individual.
It has also caught the attention of creators like Melissa Kristin, a TikTok star with more than 900,000 followers, who grew up on MySpace and remembers it as a more personal digital space.
"It was all very much your own little world, your own corner of the internet," Kristin says.
That sense of autonomy shaped how she expresses herself online today, and she believes that a revived MySpace should avoid the algorithmic, pay-to-play dynamics that dominate modern platforms.
"It would be best served for personal connection rather than performance," she says.
"Just to recapture that high we felt as millennials when we got all the friend requests and comments. It helped us feel connected."
MySpace launched in 2003 and quickly became a cultural hub, helping artists like Arctic Monkeys, Adele, and Nicki Minaj find early audiences.
But its highly customised pages, auto-playing music, and busy layouts eventually became a liability.
Facebook's cleaner, simpler design pulled users away, and MySpace struggled through redesigns and ownership changes before fading from mainstream use.
Marketing experts say any comeback will depend on learning from that history.
Dr Alexa Fox, a marketing professor at the University of Akron, says the platform was a "first mover" in social media, but one that became too complex for many users.
She believes MySpace's original strengths – music, creativity, and personal expression – could still resonate, but only with more accessible design.
"It could be more user-friendly, with less coding involved," she says.
Alex Mills, a social media strategist who has led campaigns for Spotify and Adobe, says the very thing people are nostalgic for, a feed without algorithms, was also "the thing that killed it."
"People still want a feed," Mills says. "They just want a better one than the ones optimising for rage bait."
Kevin McClary, head of performance marketing at Gorilla 76, believes MySpace should not try to compete directly with Meta, TikTok, or X.
"They can be successful and sustainable even as a niche platform," he says, arguing it should be rooted in 2000s culture.
McClary says leaning into MySpace's music identity could be a smart move, from profile songs to 2000s-themed festivals and merchandise.
He believes the audience could be broader than former users, with younger generations embracing the early-2000s aesthetics they never experienced firsthand.
"You see younger generations now buying old point-and-shoot digital cameras, MP3 players, even film cameras," McClary says. "They clearly have an interest in the past."
MySpace could meet users where that trend is growing by becoming a place rooted in a "specific time," he says. He noted that creators making 2000s-style content on other platforms are often at the "mercy" of algorithms.
Fox agrees that differentiation is essential.
"MySpace shouldn't hang their hat on features other platforms already dominate," Fox says, pointing to Reels and short-form videos.
Popular formats can be added, she says, but they should not define the platform.
She also sees an opportunity to offer a calmer experience. Today's feeds, she notes, are "algorithmic-driven AI, constantly in your face."
A platform where users have more control, or simply feel less overwhelmed, could stand out in a crowded market.
For fans like Hawkins and Kristin, the appeal is emotional as much as practical. Both say they would return if MySpace kept its original spirit.
For now, its comeback exists mostly as a promise – a reminder of a time when social media felt a little less polished and a lot more personal.
"Are you still gonna have that same feeling?" Hawkins says. "Are you still gonna feel like, 'oh my god, somebody loves me?'"

title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
summary: FOI requests reveal Banksy artworks have cost taxpayers almost £150,000, with costs still rising.
full_text:
Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
- Published
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost £150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.
The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than £85,000.
The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent £50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further £35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.
The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.
More from Bristol
Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.
The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.
Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.
Costs mount at Royal Courts
A HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS) spokesperson said: "The Royal Courts of Justice is a listed building and HMCTS are obliged to maintain its original character."
The Metropolitan Police have confirmed: "On Monday, 8 September officers received a report of criminal damage to the side of the Royal Courts of Justice.
"At this time, no arrests have been made and the investigation remains ongoing."
Court staff barricaded off the area and guarded it. Attempts to clean off the mural began immediately.
But the fact he has painted on an historic court has divided opinion.
Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy said: "It's outrageous that tens of thousands of pounds of taxpayers' money – maybe more – will have to be spent cleaning up after Banksy, who seems to believe he has a right to deface public buildings with impunity.
"Our courts are a national symbol of justice and the rule of law.
"Banksy's vandalism should be stopped and he should foot the bill for the costs he imposes on others."
However, art critic Estelle Lovatt defended Banksy's work and pointed to the benefits for tourism: "Some people visit Buckingham Palace and others visit Banksy's art.
"His work brings people together in a way that politics can divide us. He's like the Pied Piper or a town crier.
"It can be intimidating if a mural appears on your building, in terms of the crowds, but he makes art accessible because there's no gallery fee."
It's not the first time Banksy has painted on a listed building.
His early works in Bristol included a mural of a man hanging from a window, on a Georgian house.
First attempts to scrub off the paint on the court were not completely successful, so contractors have been on site using "laser technology".
Westminster City Council will have to inspect the wall and if the removal is deemed incomplete, another cleaning method will have to be used.
As a final option, the affected stonework may have to be removed and replaced.
A Listed Building Consent (LBC) application has been submitted for the installation of railings across the wall that Banksy targeted.
If approval is granted then the costs to install the railings are not yet known.
Previous works incurred expenses
The court mural is not the first of Banksy's works to create costs for public bodies.
In April, a statue of a man carrying a flag appeared in Waterloo Place near Trafalgar Square.
The flag covers the man's face and he appears to be about to step and fall from the plinth.
Banksy claimed responsibility with a video on Instagram showing the night-time installation.
Westminster City Council, which owns the land, says it had no prior knowledge of the statue.
The authority said it had spent almost £60,000 on safety barriers, administration and paying for a security guard to keep watch over it.
In response to a Freedom of Information request, Westminster Council said: "Ownership of the statue now sits with the council as landowner.
"The council has notified the artist's agent that it is reviewing options for the short, medium and long term."
The BBC has asked for more clarification on this statement.
In August 2024, Banksy painted piranha fish on a City of London Police sentry box.
The sentry box had been installed in the 1990s as part of security measures introduced after IRA attacks in the City of London.
After Banksy painted it, the box was removed at a cost of £2,200 and was never replaced.
It was put in storage and is due to be displayed at the London Museum when it reopens in November.
The works are a reminder of Banksy's continuing influence more than three decades after he first became known in Bristol, where surviving murals remain among the city's best-known tourist attractions.

title: Tonnes of rotting food from vast LA warehouse fire creates unbearable stench
summary: A fire destroyed a warehouse, leaving heaps of rotting chicken, poultry and fish to attract flies and rats.
full_text:
Tonnes of rotting food from vast LA warehouse fire creates unbearable stench
- Published
On any typical day, Alexis Sicairos and his girlfriend have a line of patrons waiting to order a banana buzz latte or a cloud matcha at their Los Angeles coffee stand. But now, the street corner where they sit is largely empty.
The reason is clear the second you walk into the neighbourhood: it stinks.
On 17 June, a fire destroyed a large cold-storage warehouse in the area, leaving behind some 85 million lb (39 million kg) of rotting food, including beef, pork, poultry and seafood.
Nearly two months later, residents of Boyle Heights say the clean-up has taken a lot longer than expected, and they've grown frustrated with the pungent odour hovering over the area.
"It smells really bad, like really bad ... to the point that you want to throw up," says Mesha, a 37-year-old security guard stationed outside a marijuana dispensary.
She likens the smell to that of a dead body.
Lineage, the company that operated the warehouse, said that as of Monday about 80% of the food waste had been removed. But city officials said this week that the company's response "has fallen short", and that they have issued public health and safety violation notices.
"It's been tough," Sicairos, 30, says. After shutting down his coffee stand for two weeks because of the fire, Brew Sting has reopened - but the demand hasn't been the same.
He says flies have been swarming relentlessly over the past weeks, since the food that was stored in the warehouse began rotting.
The warehouse workers that would previously line up to buy coffee haven't been showing up over the past two months.
"Due to the fire, obviously most of them aren't here," Sicairos says. "So we lost those customers, but we also lost customers that don't want to be around the smell, the smoke, the flies. It's understandable. But we have to keep paying our bills, so we're still here."
One cannot walk through the area, which is mostly a warehouse district surrounded by homes, without swatting away countless flies, both big and small, including black, blue and green ones.
As Sicairos packs up his coffee stand for the day, flies are landing on his tables and his body. He acknowledges that patrons don't want to see flies when they're purchasing food or drinks to consume.
A city-commissioned inspection report found that waste and high temperatures at the warehouse could speed up the breeding of flies capable of infecting wounds in both people and animals, a local NBC affiliate reported, external.
The report from a pest control company said it could put people and animals with open wounds at risk of contracting disease.
People in the community have also reported seeing large rats, and they say traps placed along sidewalks aren't big enough to hold them.
Many residents blame the city for what they deem an inadequate response to the fire and a lack of transparency and resources.
"I understand why residents are frustrated," Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass told the BBC in a statement. "They deserve transparency, clear communication, and meaningful support. Since day one, I have been in Boyle Heights listening to residents, meeting with families, and making sure their voices guide our response."
The mayor, who is up for re-election this year, said she directed city departments to work with local, state, federal, nonprofit and community partners to deliver immediate support and solutions.
Bass has also issued executive orders to mobilise resources and speed up the cleaning process. The city says they and other local partners have brought mobile health clinics to the neighbourhood and delivered thousands of air purifiers.
Late last month, the county's public health department fined Lineage for "unsanitary and nuisance" conditions with $500-a-day citations.
The mayor has given Lineage a 13 August deadline to complete the cleanup. The company said on Monday they are 80% of the way there - up from 60% on July 31.
"Our goal is to complete bulk food waste removal from the site next week," a Lineage spokesperson told the BBC on Wednesday. They expect to spend between $80 million to $100 million on the cleanup.
Outside the warehouse, dozens of workers in hard hats and neon vests can be seen tackling the effort, some wearing face coverings. Officials with the local air quality authority and sheriff's office were also on site.
In an letter shared on Tuesday, Bass said the company's response "has fallen short".
"Residents, public agencies, and elected officials have repeatedly sought timely information regarding the cleanup, remediation, environmental monitoring, and recovery," Bass wrote in the letter to Lineage shareholders. "Too often, those requests have been met with delayed communication, limited transparency, and insufficient public engagement".
The mayor also directed city departments to halt plans to rebuild the warehouse "until the health and safety of the community are protected".
Lineage, which is a temperature-controlled warehousing and logistics company, says "cleanup crews are working around the clock to remove food waste, clear debris and dismantle damaged sections of the structure.
"However, this is a highly complex operation," they say, adding that reducing odours is a "key priority" in their cleanup effort.

title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
summary: The government is trying to attribute blame for the unprecedented fires which tore through the country last month.
full_text:
Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
- Published
After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: Why?
A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.
But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.
The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.
In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a €150,000 (£128,000) fine, if convicted.
Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Étape forest in the Vosges region.
"Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est Républicain, the newspaper that reported the story.
Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts.
"I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.
The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.
The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.
But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances.
"The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying.
Working out how a fire started is, unsurprisingly, not easy.
"In periods of drought such as this one, all you need is a simple lighter," explains Eric Dufayet, an officer who investigates fires.
Once a fire is out, Eric's first task is to map its outline along the edge of the burnt vegetation, then trace it back to its point of origin. If the wind has been steady, that outline often forms a "V" shape. From there, his team works backwards along the path the flames took.
"If someone deliberately starts a fire, they may not have used only one device," he says. It improves the chances of a DNA or fingerprint sample being found.
Experts believe arson accounts for only a small fraction of fires. Most are believed to be accidental, with sparks potentially coming from construction work, faulty electrical equipment, cigarette butts and barbecues.
"With cigarettes, it's called the '30' rule," says Eric Dufayet. To start a fire, he explains, there must be "a temperature of at least 30C (86F), a maximum of 30% humidity, wind of less than 30km/h (19mph), and at least 30% of the cigarette unburnt."
In the current drought, he says it is even easier. If those conditions are met, a fire can easily spread, and fast.
According to Michel Lejoyeux, a professor of psychiatry and addictive behaviour at Paris 7 University, people who start fires fall into three categories: those who are careless, those who benefit - with an insurance payout, for example - and pyromaniacs.
"The pyromaniac doesn't get money, has no spirit of revenge, has no utility of the fire, but he likes the fire," he says.
However, pyromania is a rare psychiatric disorder that Lejoyeux says is very difficult to diagnose, and accounts for few arson convictions.
Lawyer Muriel Gestas, who has handled several such cases, says some firefighters alleged to have started fires may have wanted to be seen as saviours. For others - notably volunteers earning tax-free overtime - the motive may be financial.
Amid concerns over how officials are pursuing suspects, broader worries about wildfires are far from abating. Forecasts suggest France's next heatwave is only days away.
President Emmanuel Macron says criticism should not be the priority right now. "We will have to replant and rebuild a different kind of forest because we must adapt to the structural conditions of climate change," he said this week.
"The time for reviewing lessons learned will come," he insisted. "In the meantime, the country must remain united."
Even so, the damage these fires have inflicted on the environment, hundreds of homes, tourism, local businesses and air quality has left the French public with a lot of questions.

title: Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' trip
summary: A rare turtle is being flown home to the Caribbean Sea after being found washed up in Wales.
full_text:
Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' trip
- Published
A rare turtle that washed up on a Welsh beach is being flown 5,000 miles (8,047km) back home to the Gulf of Mexico.
Rhossi the Kemp's ridley sea turtle was found close to death in December 2023, and has been nursed back to health by staff at the Anglesey Sea Zoo.
Now, conservationists have begun a carefully co-ordinated operation to fly him across the Atlantic ocean, making sure he does not dry out along the way.
"For his skin, we use KY Jelly - better known as a sex lubricant - because it's gentle on the eyes," said Matt Davidson, curator of Anglesey Sea Zoo.
It has taken almost two years to plan, including building a special temperature-controlled crate for him, and co-ordinating complex paperwork across two countries.
Rhossi normally lives in the sea, but has to travel out of the water – first by helicopter from Anglesey to London, then by cargo flight to Houston, Texas, USA.
It means the journey needs to be completed as quickly as possible, and staff have to be constantly on hand to make sure he does not dry out or dehydrate.
Davidson said: "We have to make sure that the shell is really well lubricated, so we spread Vaseline all over to stop it drying out and flaking off.
"The same for the skin – it's really delicate – and especially the eyes, which both have to be lubricated before he goes into the crate and again just before takeoff, or he will start to peel like someone getting sunburned.
"But I have had to go to the checkout in a chemist's with about eight tubes of KY Jelly and three tubs of Vaseline and explain what's happening when I get strange looks."
Rhossi got his name because he was found on a beach near Rhosneigr on Anglesey in December 2023 by a dog called Meg, out for a walk with her owner.
He was less than two years old and was only just alive, in a state that conservationists call "cold-stunned" from being in much cooler water than his normal habitat.
Staff at the Anglesey Sea Zoo believe he lost his way while in warmer seas because of strong winds.
They have cared for him over the last two-and-a-half years as he tripled in size and grew from weighing under 1kg (2.2lb) to 21kg (46lbs).
Frankie Hobro, owner of the Anglesey Sea Zoo, said: "Cold-stunned turtles rarely survive without specialist help - we didn't know if he would make it in the first week or two.
"Turtles belong in the wild, not in captivity, so it's incredibly emotional because this is what we've been working towards for more than two years.
"But we have got to know him and his individual quirks while caring for him, and we know that soon, a little piece of us is going to be swimming off into the Caribbean Sea, and we'll never see him again."
Kemp's ridleys are the rarest sea turtle in the world, and lay their eggs on only two beaches in Mexico and in Texas, USA.
The Anglesey Sea Zoo hopes that Rhossi's release back into the wild will be a small step towards the survival of the species.
Rhossi is the fourth sea turtle to be rescued and rehabilitated by the zoo over the past decade.
Staff are currently planning to build a special turtle rescue centre to care for any more sea turtles found cold-stunned around the Welsh coast.

title: Hungary nominates former Supreme Court chief Andras Baka for presidency
summary: Andras Baka, a strong advocate for judicial independence, becomes governing party's pick for Hungary's next president.
full_text:
Hungary nominates former Supreme Court chief Andras Baka for presidency
Andras Baka, a strong advocate for judicial independence, becomes Tisza’s pick for Hungary’s next president.
Hungary’s governing Tisza party has nominated Andras Baka, a former Supreme Court chief removed from his post by Viktor Orban’s government in 2012, as its candidate for the country’s presidency.
The nomination, announced Saturday by Prime Minister Peter Magyar, marks the latest step in Tisza’s effort to dismantle Orban’s influence over state institutions since the party’s landslide election victory in April ended his 16-year rule.

The decision to nominate Baka for the presidency comes weeks after Tisza used a constitutional amendment to remove Orban-era President Tamas Sulyok from office.
On Tuesday, Baka, 73, is expected to be elected by parliament, where Tisza holds a constitutional majority.
Magyar wrote on Facebook that the nomination, made by secret ballot within the party’s parliamentary group, was “one of its most important decisions so far”.
Tisza lawmakers said Baka had always “attached paramount importance to the principle of separation of powers, consistently standing up for the rule of law and judicial independence”, adding that his experience represented “a significant asset” as the party lays “the foundations for Hungary’s new constitutional order”.
Fidesz, the party now in opposition, said it would boycott the vote, accusing Tisza of authoritarian tactics – allegations it denies.
Baka served two terms as a judge on the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg before being elected head of Hungary’s Supreme Court in 2009.
He was removed two years later after publicly criticising Orban’s government reforms, which he said threatened judicial independence. The European court later ruled that his dismissal had violated his rights to a fair trial and freedom of expression, a judgement the Council of Europe said Hungary failed to fully implement.
Hungary’s presidency carries mostly ceremonial powers, with limited authority to veto or refer legislation, though the nomination is being treated as a heavily symbolic move.

title: Turkiye says Mecca defence pact not aimed at Iran
summary: Turkiye says the Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan does not target Iran.
full_text:
Turkiye says Mecca defence pact not aimed at Iran
The pact includes an Article 5-style mutual-defence clause, but questions remain over how it would operate in practice and how Tehran will respond.
Turkish leaders have insisted that the new trilateral defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan is not directed at Iran.
Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that the pact does not identify Iran, or any other country, as a common threat.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkiye defence pact challenges US role
- list 2 of 4Iran deliberates Hormuz arrangement amid uncertain prospects with US
- list 3 of 4Yemen’s government forces attack Houthis amid renewed shelling of Marib
- list 4 of 4What are the challenges facing the Mecca agreement?
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was signed on Friday by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, stating that an armed attack on one of the three countries would be considered an attack on them all.
“There is no common threat that we have put in writing,” Fidan told Turkey’s state-run Anadolu agency, adding that countries that do not attack the signatories would not be considered targets.
An Article 5-style commitment
Fidan described the pact as “technically” similar to NATO’s Article 5 collective-defence clause, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
But the response would depend on the circumstances.
A country under attack would have to request assistance and specify what kind of support it needed, Fidan said. That could range from intelligence and logistics to ammunition or the deployment of military units.
The alliance will also establish political and military committees, bringing together foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs, as well as a secretariat in Saudi Arabia.
Fidan said the three countries would work on joint training, intelligence sharing, logistics, threat assessments and military interoperability.
Defence-industry cooperation is also expected to be a notable part of the pact. Fidan said it was one of the main issues discussed by the three leaders in Mecca, including how the countries could benefit from each other’s military technologies.
The Turkish minister said preparations for the agreement had been under way for nearly two years and eight months, suggesting it was not drawn up simply in response to the current tensions involving Iran.
Iran pushes back
Despite Ankara’s assurances, some Iranian officials have questioned the agreement and warned Saudi Arabia against relying on its new partners for security.
Mahmoud Nabavian, a member of Iran’s parliamentary National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, said Saudi leaders should understand that cooperation with Turkiye and Pakistan would not guarantee their security.
Another commission member, Ebrahim Rezaei, similarly dismissed the pact as a “paper agreement”.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi did not directly mention the agreement in a message on X on Friday, but he called on regional states to rely on themselves and pursue what he described as “true brotherhood”.
At the same time, he stressed the strength and readiness of Iran’s armed forces.
Egypt could join next
Fidan portrayed the agreement as part of a broader effort to give regional countries greater responsibility for their own security.
“External hegemons coming into the region do not solve the problems; they make them more acute,” he told Anadolu.
He described Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan as the “core countries” of the initiative and made clear that Ankara wants the arrangement to expand.
“Under our president’s vision, we should not remain limited to three countries,” Fidan said. “We should grow and, if necessary, bring all countries under this umbrella.”
Several countries have already expressed interest, according to Fidan, who said he expected Egypt, which he described as a “natural partner”, to join once outstanding technical issues were resolved.
For now, many of the practical details remain to be worked out, including how the three militaries would coordinate in a crisis.
But the planned committees, permanent secretariat and focus on interoperability and defence-industry cooperation suggest the pact is intended to develop beyond a simple mutual defence declaration.

title: Solar eclipse to occur next week. Here is what to know
summary: It will be visible in parts of the U.S. on Wednesday.
full_text:
Solar eclipse to occur next week. Here is what to know
People throughout Europe and parts of the U.S. will be treated to a chance to see a solar eclipse on Wednesday.
People in Iceland, Greenland, northern Russia, Spain, and a part of Portugal will see a total eclipse, according to astronomers. That's when the moon passes between the Earth and the Sun, fully blocking the Sun's face. NASA says northern parts of the United States, including from Alaska to North Carolina, will see a partial solar eclipse.
During a partial solar eclipse, the moon passes between the sun and Earth, but the celestial bodies are not perfectly aligned. Because only parts of the sun are obscured, the sun appears as a crescent shape.
The partial eclipse is expected to begin around 1:17 p.m. ET in Washington, D.C. and have 4% coverage, according to NASA. That means up to 4 percent of the sun will be covered by the moon. In Reykjavík, Iceland, the total eclipse will begin at 5:48 p.m. local time , and in León, Spain, totality will begin at 8:28 p.m and last for two minutes. This will be the first solar eclipse visible from Spain's mainland since 1905, according to the European Space Agency.
For those who plan to watch either the total or partial eclipse, special equipment such as eclipse glasses or handheld viewers with special filters will be necessary to protect one's eyes. Regular sunglasses will not be effective for eye protection, even during a partial eclipse. Looking at the sun, even if for a short time, can cause significant eye damage, including burns and even permanent vision loss, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology.
While the eclipse will give skywatchers a chance to safely marvel at the rare phenomena, some scientists will use it as an opportunity to better understand the sun. NASA says it will have teams using scientific balloons and a high-altitude jet to study how the sky when darkened for a short period of time impacts the Earth's atmosphere.
"From our unique perspective on Earth during a total solar eclipse, scientists can study the Sun's corona in a way we can't from anywhere else in the solar system," Kelly Korreck, eclipse program manager for NASA, said in a statement.
The next partial solar eclipse will be visible across parts of the U.S. on Aug. 2, 2027 – with totality visible from Spain, the Middle East and parts of North Africa. A total solar eclipse will be visible across parts of the contiguous U.S. on Aug. 23, 2044.

title: Is China’s party newspaper carrying more stories highlighting women’s role as mothers?
summary:
“Women hold up half the sky.”
This iconic quote attributed to Mao Zedong has been central to Beijing’s messaging about gender equality for decades.
It was not just a slogan. After the founding of the People’s Republic in 1949, the Communist Party passed a Marriage Law that banned arranged marriages, abolished foot-binding and encouraged women to enter education and the workplace.
But the party’s stance on where women belong has shifted over the decades, according to a new study.
To gauge the...
full_text:
Is China’s party newspaper carrying more stories highlighting women’s role as mothers?
Analysis of 125,000 articles from People’s Daily suggests it is increasingly framing women in a domestic rather than public context
“Women hold up half the sky.”
This iconic quote attributed to Mao Zedong has been central to Beijing’s messaging about gender equality for decades.
It was not just a slogan. After the founding of the People’s Republic in 1949, the Communist Party passed a Marriage Law that banned arranged marriages, abolished foot-binding and encouraged women to enter education and the workplace.
But the party’s stance on where women belong has shifted over the decades, according to a new study.
To gauge the Communist Party’s stance on women’s role in society, researchers analysed 125,532 articles published between 1990 and 2023 in People’s Daily – the party’s mouthpiece – arguing these “directly reflect” the views of the party and central government.
They found that the paper had increasingly distanced women from their role in the public sphere in recent years while maintaining a strong focus on their role in the household.

title: 我弄丟手機後，Claude 幫我做了一個「藍牙強度追蹤器」成功找回
summary:
創建一支工具的成本正在指數型下降。一名工程師的手機翻遍辦公室找不到，最後靠 Claude 現寫的藍牙訊號強度追 […]

〈我弄丟手機後，Claude 幫我做了一個「藍牙強度追蹤器」成功找回〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
創建一支工具的成本正在指數型下降。一名工程師的手機翻遍辦公室找不到，最後靠 Claude 現寫的藍牙訊號強度追蹤器把它撈了回來。
（前情提要：Claude Opus 4.6 來了：自己寫編譯器、做 PPT、隨手挖出 500 個零日漏洞，你的工作它都想試試）
（背景補充：Anthropic 新推「回顧儀錶板」：檢視你跟 Claude 互動、教你更聰明與 AI 協作）
找不到手機的那三十分鐘，工程師 Ben 翻遍了辦公室的每個角落都毫無所獲。最後，他問了 Claude，AI 給的建議是打造一支追蹤藍牙訊號強度的小工具，並大約一分鐘就寫好了。
接著他一邊在辦公室裡走動，一邊盯著螢幕上的數字往上爬，最後還真的找到了他的手機（下面貼文可以看到他附上的尋找手機過程）。
Lost my phone at the office and spent 30 minutes turning the place over. Find My was disabled by MDM.
Out of ideas, I asked Claude how I could find it. It suggested tracking the Bluetooth signal strength, then wrote me a meter in about a minute.
I walked around watching the… pic.twitter.com/sCMUmTJIOl
— Ben Zhang (@un1c0rnioz) August 4, 2026
MDM 關掉訊號之後
許多企業會用 MDM（行動裝置管理）系統統一管理員工裝置，方便遠端安裝軟體、設定密碼原則，也方便在裝置遺失時鎖定或抹除資料。
但代價是蘋果原生的 Find My 定位功能經常被連帶關閉，對企業而言這是安全考量，但對弄丟手機的員工而言，就少了最直覺的救命工具。
這工具能做什麼？
Ben 還在 GitHub 上公開這個名為 findphone 的工具，核心原理是持續讀取藍牙裝置的 RSSI（接收訊號強度指標）。簡單來說就是，手機收到的訊號有多大聲，數字越大代表裝置離你越近。
它用 Swift 寫成，需要 macOS 13 以上才能執行，不依賴任何外部套件，用 swift build -c release 就能自行編譯；作者也附上打包成 arm64 與 x86_64 通用二進位檔的指令碼，方便不同款 Mac 直接拿來用。
工具還附上兩個貼心設計：加上 ，sound 旗標，會發出類似倒車雷達的音效，越靠近嗶得越快；加上 ，redact 旗標，則會遮蔽藍牙位址，方便錄影展示時不外洩裝置資訊。
當然，藍牙訊號定位終究不是 GPS。RSSI 的先天精度大約只有 2 到 5 公尺，就算環境理想，也很難做到 2 公尺以內；一旦遇到金屬、玻璃或水這類會造成訊號反射與繞射的環境，誤差可能超過 5 公尺，讀數甚至會不按牌理出牌。換句話說，這支工具給的是「越走越近」的方向感，不是一個精確座標，真正定位手機的還是用戶自己的雙腳。
但這個故事告訴我們：過去寫一支工具的成本，遠遠高於忍受一次麻煩。但這問題被 AI 倒過來。從前不值得為一個人開發的軟體，現在跑得通了。

title: BitMart 創辦人喊：沒跑路也不會跑路，社群甩大量「提幣卡單」截圖怒轟快還錢
summary:
BitMart 創辦人 Sheldon Xia 於昨晚發出四點聲明否認跑路，強調團隊仍在進行資產盤點、有序清退 […]

〈BitMart 創辦人喊：沒跑路也不會跑路，社群甩大量「提幣卡單」截圖怒轟快還錢〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
BitMart 創辦人 Sheldon Xia 於昨晚發出四點聲明否認跑路，強調團隊仍在進行資產盤點、有序清退。但留言區並不買帳，用戶紛紛貼出提現卡單、客服失聯與前員工欠薪等截圖反駁。
（前情提要：交易所 BitMart 宣布收攤：8/26 停止交易、2027 年初關站，兩個月前才否認提幣危機）
（背景補充：BitMart 收攤後提幣延遲，BMX 一週暴挫 81.5%，CZ 提醒：交易所關門要收購不簡單）
面對社群排山倒海的「跑路」質疑，BitMart 創辦人 Sheldon Xia 昨晚在 X 發出四點聲明。第一，否認跑路且承諾「不會跑路」；第二，呼籲用戶不要輕信「前員工爆料」等各種流傳截圖。
第三，核心團隊仍在進行資產盤點、資產歸集與系統維護，「有序清退」是團隊目標，請等待後續公告；第四，否認有挪用資產、提前搶跑或撤離等行為，並表示已考慮讓法院與第三方審計機構介入，出具透明報告。
1.我们没有跑路，也不会跑路。
2.很多谣言和所谓的前员工、现任员工所谓的爆料，截图等等，请不要轻信谣言。
3.核心团队还在进行资产盘点，资产归集和系统维护的工作，有序清退是我们的目标，请等待公告和通知。…
— Sheldon (@sheldonbitmart) August 8, 2026
社群不買單，卡單截圖一張接一張
但聲明底下，清一色是用戶的不滿。用戶 @btcexactly 開炮：「光說無用，給具體的時間表、詳細兌付方案，否則都是空話，拖延個 5 到 10 年有什麼意義？和詐騙跑路沒有區別」。
更直接的證據是提現詳情截圖。用戶 @oldtale12345 貼出的紀錄顯示，一筆 2,910.06 ALGO 的提領申請，早在 7 月 27 日 22:31:27 就已建立，狀態卻停在「已建立」，完成時間與 TXID 全部空白。
另一名用戶 @ys_chen 的截圖也是同樣劇本：1,122.05016 USDT-TRX 的提現單在 7 月 27 日 11:52:45 建立後，同樣卡在 Created 狀態，沒有完成時間、也沒有交易雜湊。
自稱前員工的 @MetaMarshmello 留言更直白：「到現在你發給我們的薪水都還提不了款。」
官方時間表 vs 用戶體感
根據 BitMart 官方公告的時間表，7 月 26 日 09:30 起停止新用戶註冊；8 月 26 日 15:59（UTC）全面停止交易服務，持倉須在當日 01:00（UTC）前平倉；提現申請的最後受理時間點是 8 月 26 日 05:00（UTC）；平台預計 2027 年 1 月 31 日正式關閉。
但問題在於，官方給的是提現的「截止日」，用戶真正需要的則是提現的「完成日」。而且社群指出，每日提現額度被壓到 2,000 美元、各鏈手續費也同時大幅調高，「這種行為非常不厚道，讓用戶非常恐慌」。
隨著 8 月 26 日的提現受理截止日將近，BitMart 能否在期限內端出具體時間表與審計報告，將是決定這場信任危機走向的關鍵。

title: 俄羅斯硬體錢包銷量翻倍！新法 9/1 生效，散戶急轉向自託管
summary:
俄羅斯兩大零售商 Q2 硬體錢包銷量暴增 84-107%，9 月 1 日新加密法規生效前，散戶搶先布局自託管。 […]

〈俄羅斯硬體錢包銷量翻倍！新法 9/1 生效，散戶急轉向自託管〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
俄羅斯兩大零售商 Q2 硬體錢包銷量暴增 84-107%，9 月 1 日新加密法規生效前，散戶搶先布局自託管。但非託管錢包仍無法繞過提領限制。
（前情提要：普丁簽署加密專法！核心條款 9/1 生效，與數位盧布強制上路同天）
（背景補充：俄羅斯國家杜馬今日決議加密貨幣法案！散戶年限買 30 萬盧布，最快 9/1 生效）
俄羅斯散戶在加密法規生效前，持續買入了硬體錢包。根據當地兩大電商 M.Video 與 Wildberries 公布的資料，2026 年上半年俄羅斯硬體錢包銷售量翻倍以上成長，銷售金額也大幅攀升。
這波買氣出現在 9 月 1 日新加密法規生效前，反映俄羅斯投資者對自託管的關注急遽上升。
資料：兩家零售商的銷售爆炸
根據兩家零售商資料，呈現以下趨勢：
- M.Video（俄羅斯最大電子產品零售商之一）：2026 Q2 硬體錢包銷量較 Q1 成長 107%，銷售金額成長 92%
- Wildberries（電商平台，母公司 RWB）：2026 H1 銷量較 2025 H1 成長 84%，銷售金額成長 60%
- Wildberries 上硬體錢包平均價格從約 9,050 盧布降至 7,900 盧布（跌幅 13%），價格下探刺激更多買氣
M.Video 同時擴大硬體錢包產品線，不過兩家平台都未說明銷量暴增的具體原因。
新法 9/1 生效：散戶能買，但不能隨便轉
這波硬體錢包買氣推測與俄羅斯即將生效的加密法規直接相關。9 月 1 日起，俄羅斯新版加密貨幣框架正式實施，核心內容包括：
- 允許受監管的加密交易所與數位存放處營運
- 部分散戶在完成測試後可購買流動性加密貨幣，每年上限 30 萬盧布（約 3,100 美元）／每家中介機構
- 繼續禁止在境內以加密貨幣進行支付（央行明確保留此禁令）
- 過渡期（至 2027 年 7 月 1 日）結束後，所有加密交易必須透過受監管實體進行，銀行拒絕處理框架外的交易
換句話說，俄羅斯散戶在新法下可以合法持有加密資產，但使用場景仍然受限。這也解釋了為什麼硬體錢包需求上升，散戶傾向把資產握在自己手上，而非放在受監管的中介平台。
硬體錢包合法，但提領仍有限制
根據俄羅斯法律顧問對 RBC 的說法，非託管錢包（non-custodial wallet）本身並不違法。但關鍵限制在於：
- 從俄羅斯數位存放處提領至個人錢包是被禁止的（過渡期至 2027/7/1）
- 過渡期結束後，提領必須透過受監管實體
換言之，新法生效後買了硬體錢包無法繞過提領限制，因此大量用戶選擇在剩下的時間趕緊轉移資產。
後續觀察
俄羅斯這波硬體錢包銷量暴增，反映加密市場一個長期趨勢：在監管框架逐漸成形的前夕，散戶會優先確保資產掌控權。但有三點值得關注：
- 30 萬盧布年購上限對大多數散戶而言偏低，能否支撐持續的加密資產需求？
- 受監管交易所與數位存放處的合規門檻如何設計，將決定俄羅斯加密生態的品質
- 在國際制裁背景下，俄羅斯散戶透過加密貨幣進行跨境資產配置的動機是否會推升硬體錢包長期需求？

title: Bitwise 投資長：兆元機構資金即將流入比特幣，2035 年上看 130 萬美元
summary:
Bitwise 投資長 Matt Hougan 預測，未來十年將有兆元級機構資金流入比特幣。他指出全球大型機構 […]

〈Bitwise 投資長：兆元機構資金即將流入比特幣，2035 年上看 130 萬美元〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
Bitwise 投資長 Matt Hougan 預測，未來十年將有兆元級機構資金流入比特幣。他指出全球大型機構控制 100-200 兆美元資產，只要 1% 配置比特幣，就足以支撐每枚 130 萬美元的長期價格目標。
（前情提要：比特幣將漲到百萬美元！Bitwise 投資長：關鍵不在時間，在於搶下多少財富市場份額）
（背景補充：機構資金瘋買比特幣！全球散戶卻「反應冷淡」？）
比特幣投資機構 Bitwise 首席投資長 Matt Hougan 近日向 CoinDesk 表示，比特幣在未來十年將吸引兆元級機構資金，價格可能攀升至 130 萬美元。Hougan 的分析建立在一個簡單的假設：全球大型機構只需將資產組合的 1% 配置到比特幣。
1% 配置，就足以支撐 130 萬美元
根據 Hougan 的估算，全球退休基金、捐贈基金、保險公司、主權基金與央行合計控制約 100 兆到 200 兆美元 的資產。這些機構若將僅 1% 的資產配置比特幣，流入的資金規模足以支撐他設定的長期價格目標。
Hougan 的 130 萬美元目標建立在比特幣與黃金「儲值市場」的份額競爭上。他在 CoinDesk 的訪談中說明：
- 黃金 ETF 於 2004 年上線時，黃金市值約 2 兆美元，如今已增長至約 30 兆美元
- 過去 20 年黃金市值平均年增率約 13%
- 若未來十年仍以這個速度成長，儲值市場的總規模將大幅擴張
- 比特幣若拿下該市場的 25% 份額，每枚價格將來到 130 萬美元
市場上常見的說法是「比特幣取代黃金 50%」，以此算出每枚約 71.5 萬美元。Hougan 認為這個演算法過於保守，儲值市場本身仍在擴張，比特幣不必「吃掉」黃金的份額，只要分一杯羹就已足夠。
第一波機構資金已經進場
Hougan 指出，最早大規模配置比特幣的專業投資者會是財務顧問與家族辦公室。他認為這個轉變已經可見端倪：
美國 SEC 的 13F 申報（大型投資管理機構季報）中，已經可以看到比特幣現貨 ETF 的持倉增長。同時，Morgan Stanley 與 Wells Fargo 等大型財富管理機構也已開始讓客戶更容易接觸比特幣。
「這是個超過 10 年的過程，」Hougan 強調。
從 Strategy 到退休基金：需求動力的世代交替
Strategy（微策略）長期被視為比特幣最大的企業買家，目前持有 842,138 BTC。但 Hougan 認為，Strategy 已不再是比特幣需求的主要推手。
他指出，Michael Saylor 的比特幣購買引擎過去依賴兩個「資本市場錯置」：
- 投資人曾把 Strategy 的股票視為少數能在公開市場取得加密曝險的方式，讓公司能以高於比特幣持倉淨值的溢價發新股
- 公司接著利用可轉換債券與特別股發行，募集更多資金投入比特幣
但這兩個優勢都已減弱。比特幣現貨 ETF 上線後，投資人有了更直接的曝險工具，Strategy 難以維持溢價。同時，公司已經發行了市場願意承受的債務上限。
「輕鬆的累積路徑已經耗盡」Hougan 說。他認為 Strategy 仍會繼續買入，但速度會慢下來，且更貼近價格週期。
更好的問題不是底在哪，而是頂還沒到吧
Hougan 對長線投資者的建議很直白：
不用擔心比特幣是否找到區域性底部，更值得思考的是，更好的問題是，頂點是否已經來到。
他認為加密資產從零成長到 2 兆美元市值，靠的是散戶。但如果要從 2 兆跳到 20 兆，帶領者必然是機構資金。而這些機構，才剛開始動。

title: 比特幣 ETF 單週吸金十億美元創 4 月新高，Coldcard 錢包漏洞效應浮現？
summary:
本週美國現貨比特幣 ETF 淨流入約 10 億美元，為今年 4 月以來最佳單周表現。Bloomberg 分析師 […]

〈比特幣 ETF 單週吸金十億美元創 4 月新高，Coldcard 錢包漏洞效應浮現？〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
本週美國現貨比特幣 ETF 淨流入約 10 億美元，為今年 4 月以來最佳單周表現。Bloomberg 分析師 Eric Balchunas 認為，Coldcard 硬體錢包漏洞事件長期可能吸引更多投資者轉向 ETF，將自託管的風險與技術門檻交給專業機構承擔。
（前情提要：Coldcard MK3 冷錢包爆「種子漏洞」：594 枚比特幣 25 分鐘掃空）
（背景補充：Coldcard 漏洞引起恐慌，12 萬枚 BTC 轉移錢包地址）
美國現貨比特幣 ETF 本週資金流出現顯著反彈。根據 Bloomberg ETF 分析師 Eric Balchunas 在 X 平台發布的資料，本週現貨基金總計吸引約 10 億美元淨流入，這是自今年 4 月以來最佳的單周表現，也是去年 10 月以來第三高的單週成績。
Balchunas 將去年 10 月形容為比特幣的「silent IPO」時期。這個概念由投資人 Jordi Visser 在 11 月的分析文章中 推廣，描述的是比特幣持有者結構正在發生根本性的轉換。
The bitcoin ETFs just clocked their best week in flows (about $1b) since April and the 3rd best week since the good ole days were ruined by the Silent IPO last Oct. IBIT, FBTC and few others saw inflows every single day since Coldcard hack, making it hard not to see causation in… pic.twitter.com/5GnmkvD5g4
— Eric Balchunas (@EricBalchunas) August 8, 2026
Silent IPO 理論：早期持有者退場、機構進場
根據 Visser 的理論，早期比特幣投資者（OG holders）在這一輪週期中逐步賣出，買方則來自 ETF 和其他機構投資者。早期持有者的賣出供給，恰好填補了機構進場的新需求，因此儘管市場有大量新資金流入，比特幣價格仍相對平穩。
不過相比去年 10 月 silent IPO 高峰期的強勁流入，今年五月以來，資金流出現顯著的下降與反覆。這使得本週 10 億美元的回彈尤為顯著，暗示機構需求可能正在重新啟動。
Coldcard 漏洞：自託管風險浮現
本週 ETF 資金流反彈的另一個背景，是動區此前多次報導的 Coldcard 硬體錢包的安全漏洞事件。Coldcard 是由 Coinkite 開發的比特幣硬體錢包，近期被發現存在韌體層面的漏洞，影響部分裝置生成錢包金鑰的機制。攻擊者利用此漏洞竊取了約 594 枚比特幣（市值約 1.16 億美元）。
此事件引發了廣泛的鏈上遷移活動。根據鏈上分析資料，約 12 萬枚長期休眠的比特幣因 Coldcard 漏洞而轉移錢包地址。
長期來看，ETF 可能從自託管風險中獲益
Balchunas 在本週的分析 中提出，Coldcard 事件可能從長期角度加強現貨比特幣 ETF 的吸引力。他的邏輯很直接：對於不願或無法承擔自託管技術風險的投資者而言，ETF 提供了機構級別的託管與安全保障。
他同時強調，相關性不等於因果關係，本週 ETF 資金流入與 Coldcard 漏洞之間沒有已證實的直接聯絡。但他的判斷是：「長期來看，我無法想像不會有一部分人選擇遷移過來。」
